Note first that the condition of the theorem implies that there are no cycles of length 4 in $G$. Let us call this the \emph{$C_4$-condition}. We first prove that any two \emph{nonadjacent} vertices $u$ and $v$ have equal degree $d(u) = d(v)$. Suppose $d(u) = k$, where $w_1, \dots, w_k$ are the neighbors of $u$. Exactly one of the $w_i$, say $w_2$, is adjacent to $v$, and $w_2$ is adjacent to exactly one of the other $w_i$'s, say $w_1$, so that we have the situation of the figure to the left. The vertex $v$ has with $w_1$ the common neighbor $w_2$, and with $w_i$ $(i \geq 2)$ a common neighbor $z_i$ $(i \geq 2)$. By the $C_4$-condition, all these $z_i$ must be distinct. We conclude $d(v) \geq k = d(u)$, and thus $d(u) = d(v) = k$ by symmetry. To finish the proof of (1), observe that any vertex different from $w_2$ is not adjacent to either $u$ or $v$, and hence has degree $k$, by what we already proved. But since $w_2$ also has a non-neighbor, it has degree $k$ as well, and thus $G$ is $k$-regular.
nodes.statement_short: A counterexample to the friendship theorem is a regular graph.

nodes.name: Rational square roots of naturals are integers
nodes.statement: Now if the square root $\sqrt{m}$ of a natural number $m$ is rational, then it is an integer!
assumptions: if the square root $\sqrt{m}$ of a natural number $m$ is rational
conclusions: then it is an integer!

nodes.name: Dedekind's proof that rational square roots are integers
nodes.statement: An elegant proof for this was presented by Dedekind in 1858: Let $n_0$ be the smallest natural number with $n_0 \sqrt{m} \in \mathbb{N}$. If $\sqrt{m} \not\in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $0 < \sqrt{m} - \ell < 1$. Setting $n_1 := n_0(\sqrt{m} - \ell)$, we find $n_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n_1 \sqrt{m} = n_0 (\sqrt{m} - \ell) \sqrt{m} = n_0 m - \ell (n_0 \sqrt{m}) \in \mathbb{N}$. With $n_1 < n_0$ this yields a contradiction to the choice of $n_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the least n_0 with n_0 sqrt(m) integral; n_1 = n_0(sqrt m - ℓ) is smaller with the same property.

nodes.name: Families of at most 2^{d-1} d-sets are 2-colorable
nodes.statement: Every family of at most $2^{d-1}$ $d$-sets is $2$-colorable, that is, $m(d) > 2^{d-1}$.
conclusions: Every family of at most $2^{d-1}$ $d$-sets is $2$-colorable, that is, $m(d) > 2^{d-1}$.
also_stated_at: Every family of at most $2^{d-1}$ $d$-sets is $2$-colorable, that is, $m(d) > 2^{d-1}$.
nodes.label: ch45theorem2

nodes.name: Graphs of large girth and chromatic number
nodes.statement: For every $k \geq 2$, there exists a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G) > k$ and girth $\gamma(G) > k$.
assumptions: For every $k \geq 2$
conclusions: there exists a graph $G$ with chromatic number $\chi(G) > k$ and girth $\gamma(G) > k$.
nodes.label: ch45theorem3

nodes.name: Crossing lemma
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a simple graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, where $m \ge 4n$. Then \[ \mycr(G) \ge \frac{1}{64}\frac{m^3}{n^2}. \]
assumptions: Let $G$ be a simple graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, where $m \ge 4n$.
conclusions: \mycr(G) \ge \frac{1}{64}\frac{m^3}{n^2}.
nodes.label: ch45theorem4

nodes.name: Form n = p_1...p_r + 1 and take a prime divisor p
nodes.statement: For any finite set $\{p_1, \dots, p_r\}$ of primes, consider the number $n = p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r + 1$. This $n$ has a prime divisor $p$.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Form n = p_1...p_r + 1 and take a prime divisor p

nodes.name: p cannot be some p_i, else p divides 1
nodes.statement: But $p$ is not one of the $p_i$'s: otherwise $p$ would be a divisor of $n$ and of the product $p_1p_2\dots p_r$, and thus also of the difference $n - p_1 p_2 \cdots p_r = 1$, which is impossible.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: p cannot be some p_i, else p divides 1

nodes.name: No finite set contains all primes
nodes.statement: So a finite set $\{p_1, \dots, p_r\}$ cannot be the collection of \emph{all} prime numbers.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: No finite set contains all primes

nodes.name: Reduce coprimality to the recursion prod F_k = F_n - 2
nodes.statement: Let us first look at the Fermat numbers \(F_n = 2^{2^n} +1\) for \(n = 0,1,2,\dots\). We will show that any two Fermat numbers are relatively prime; hence there must be infinitely many primes. To this end, we verify the recursion \[ \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} F_k = F_n - 2, \] from which our assertion follows immediately.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Reduce coprimality to the recursion prod F_k = F_n - 2

nodes.name: A common divisor divides 2, impossible since Fermat numbers are odd
nodes.statement: Indeed, if \(m\) is a divisor of, say, \(F_k\) and \(F_n\) (with \(k < n\)), then \(m\) divides 2, and hence \(m = 1\) or \(2\). But \(m = 2\) is impossible since all Fermat numbers are odd.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: A common divisor divides 2, impossible since Fermat numbers are odd

nodes.name: Base case n = 1
nodes.statement: To prove the recursion we use induction on \(n\). For \(n = 1\), we have \(F_0 = 3\) and \(F_1 - 2 = 3\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Base case n = 1

nodes.name: Inductive step via (F_n - 2)F_n = F_{n+1} - 2
nodes.statement: With induction we now conclude \[ \prod_{k=0}^{n} F_k = \left( \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} F_k \right) F_n = (F_n - 2)F_n = (2^{2^n} - 1)(2^{2^n} + 1) = 2^{2^{n+1}} - 1 = F_{n+1} - 2. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via (F_n - 2)F_n = F_{n+1} - 2

nodes.name: Assume a largest prime p; consider 2^p - 1
nodes.statement: Suppose \(\mathbb{P}\) is finite and \(p\) is the largest prime. We consider the so-called \emph{Mersenne number} \(2^p - 1\) and show that any prime factor \(q\) of \(2^p - 1\) is bigger than \(p\), which will yield the desired conclusion.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Assume a largest prime p; consider 2^p - 1

nodes.name: 2 has order p in the multiplicative group of Z_q
nodes.statement: Let \(q\) be a prime dividing \(2^p - 1\), so we have \(2^p \equiv 1 \pmod{q}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this means that the element 2 has order \(p\) in the multiplicative group \(\mathbb{Z}_q \setminus \{0\}\) of the field \(\mathbb{Z}_q\). This group has \(q - 1\) elements.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: 2 has order p in the multiplicative group of Z_q

nodes.name: Lagrange gives p | q - 1, so q > p
nodes.statement: By Lagrange's theorem, we know that the order of every element divides the size of the group, that is, we have \(p \mid q - 1\), and hence \(p < q\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Lagrange gives p | q - 1, so q > p

nodes.name: Introduce pi(x), the primes in order and log x
nodes.statement: Let \(\pi(x) := \#\{p \leq x : p \in \mathbb{P}\}\) be the number of primes that are less than or equal to the real number \(x\). We number the primes \(\mathbb{P} = \{p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots \}\) in increasing order. Consider the natural logarithm \(\log x\), defined as \[ \log x = \int_1^x \frac{1}{t} dt. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Introduce pi(x), the primes in order and log x

nodes.name: Step-function comparison bounds log x by a sum over m with prime divis
nodes.statement: Now we compare the area below the graph of \(f(t) = \frac{1}{t}\) with an upper step function. (See also the appendix for this method.) Thus for \(n \leq x < n+1\) we have \[ \log x \leq 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \dots + \frac{1}{n-1} + \frac{1}{n} \leq \sum \frac{1}{m}, \] where the sum extends over all \(m \in \mathbb{N}\) which have only prime divisors \(p \leq x\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Step-function comparison bounds log x by a sum over m with prime divisors <= x

nodes.name: Unique factorization and geometric series give a product over primes
nodes.statement: Since every such \(m\) can be written in a unique way as a product of the form \(\prod_{p \leq x} p^{k_p}\), we see that the last sum is equal to \[ \prod_{p \in \mathbb{P}, p \leq x} \left( \sum_{k \geq 0} \frac{1}{p^k} \right). \] The inner sum is a geometric series with ratio \(\frac{1}{p}\), hence \[ \log x \leq \prod_{p \leq x} \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{p}} = \prod_{p \leq x} \frac{p}{p - 1} = \prod_{k=1}^{\pi(x)} \frac{p_k}{p_k - 1}. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Unique factorization and geometric series give a product over primes

nodes.name: p_k >= k+1 yields log x <= pi(x) + 1
nodes.statement: Now clearly \(p_k \geq k+1\), and thus \[ \frac{p_k}{p_k - 1} = 1 + \frac{1}{p_k - 1} \leq 1 + \frac{1}{k} = \frac{k+1}{k}, \] and therefore \[ \log x \leq \prod_{k=1}^{\pi(x)} \frac{k+1}{k} = \pi(x) + 1. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: p_k >= k+1 yields log x <= pi(x) + 1

nodes.name: log x unbounded, so pi(x) unbounded
nodes.statement: Everybody knows that \(\log x\) is not bounded, so we conclude that \(\pi(x)\) is unbounded as well, and so there are infinitely many primes.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: log x unbounded, so pi(x) unbounded

nodes.name: Define the progressions N_{a,b} and the open sets
nodes.statement: Consider the following curious topology on the set \(\mathbb{Z}\) of integers. For \(a, b \in \mathbb{Z}, b > 0\), we set \[ N_{a,b} = \{a + nb : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}. \] Each set \(N_{a,b}\) is a two-way infinite arithmetic progression. Now call a set \(O \subseteq \mathbb{Z}\) open if either \(O\) is empty, or if to every \(a \in O\) there exists some \(b > 0\) with \(N_{a,b} \subseteq O\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Define the progressions N_{a,b} and the open sets

nodes.name: Check the topology axioms
nodes.statement: Clearly, the union of open sets is open again. If \(O_1, O_2\) are open, and \(a \in O_1 \cap O_2\) with \(N_{a,b_1} \subseteq O_1\) and \(N_{a,b_2} \subseteq O_2\), then \(a \in N_{a, b_1 b_2} \subseteq O_1 \cap O_2\). So we conclude that any finite intersection of open sets is again open. Therefore, this family of open sets induces a bona fide topology on \(\mathbb{Z}\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Check the topology axioms

nodes.name: Two facts: open sets infinite, N_{a,b} closed
nodes.statement: Let us note two facts: \begin{itemize} \item[(A)] Any nonempty open set is infinite. \item[(B)] Any set \(N_{a,b}\) is closed as well. \end{itemize} Indeed, the first fact follows from the definition. For the second, we observe \[ N_{a,b} = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{b-1} N_{a+i,b}, \] which proves that \(N_{a,b}\) is the complement of an open set and hence closed.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Two facts: open sets infinite, N_{a,b} closed

nodes.name: (A) nonempty open sets are infinite
nodes.statement: [(A)] Any nonempty open set is infinite.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: (A) nonempty open sets are infinite

nodes.name: (B) N_{a,b} is closed
nodes.statement: [(B)] Any set \(N_{a,b}\) is closed as well.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: (B) N_{a,b} is closed

nodes.name: Justify (A) and (B)
nodes.statement: Indeed, the first fact follows from the definition. For the second, we observe \[ N_{a,b} = \mathbb{Z} \setminus \bigcup_{i=1}^{b-1} N_{a+i,b}, \] which proves that \(N_{a,b}\) is the complement of an open set and hence closed.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Justify (A) and (B)

nodes.name: Z minus {1,-1} is the union of N_{0,p}
nodes.statement: So far, the primes have not yet entered the picture — but here they come. Since any number \(n \neq 1, -1\) has a prime divisor \(p\), and hence is contained in \(N_{0,p}\), we conclude \[ \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{1, -1\} = \bigcup_{p \in \mathbb{P}} N_{0,p}. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Z minus {1,-1} is the union of N_{0,p}

nodes.name: Finitely many primes would make {1,-1} open, contradicting (A)
nodes.statement: Now if \(\mathbb{P}\) were finite, then \(\bigcup_{p \in \mathbb{P}} N_{0,p}\) would be a finite union of closed sets (by (B)), and hence closed. Consequently, \(\{1, -1\}\) would be an open set, in violation of (A).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Finitely many primes would make {1,-1} open, contradicting (A)

nodes.name: Context: Erdős' proof of divergence
nodes.statement: Our final proof goes a considerable step further and demonstrates not only that there are infinitely many primes, but also that the series \(\sum_{p \in \mathbb{P}} \frac{1}{p}\) diverges. The first proof of this important result was given by Euler (and is interesting in its own right), but our proof, devised by Erdős, is of compelling beauty.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Context: Erdős' proof of divergence

nodes.name: Assume convergence; split into small and big primes
nodes.statement: Let \(p_1, p_2, p_3, \dots\) be the sequence of primes in increasing order, and assume that \(\sum_{p \in \mathbb{P}} \frac{1}{p}\) converges. Then there must be a natural number \(k\) such that \(\sum_{i \geq k+1} \frac{1}{p_i} < \frac{1}{2}\). Let us call \(p_1, \dots, p_k\) the small primes, and \(p_{k+1}, p_{k+2}, \dots\) the big primes. For an arbitrary natural number \(N\), we therefore find \[ \sum_{i \geq k+1} \frac{N}{p_i} < \frac{N}{2}. \tag{1} \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Assume convergence; split into small and big primes

nodes.name: Introduce N_b and N_s; aim for N_b + N_s < N
nodes.statement: Let \(N_b\) be the number of positive integers \(n \leq N\) which are divisible by at least one big prime, and \(N_s\) the number of positive integers \(n \leq N\) which have only small prime divisors. We are going to show that for a suitable \(N\) \[ N_b + N_s < N, \] which will be our desired contradiction, since by definition \(N_b + N_s\) would have to be equal to \(N\).
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Introduce N_b and N_s; aim for N_b + N_s < N

nodes.name: N_b < N/2
nodes.statement: To estimate \(N_b\), note that \(\left\lfloor \frac{N}{p_i} \right\rfloor\) counts the positive integers \(n \leq N\) which are multiples of \(p_i\). Hence by (1) we obtain \[ N_b \leq \sum_{i \geq k+1} \left\lfloor \frac{N}{p_i} \right\rfloor < \frac{N}{2}. \tag{2} \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: N_b < N/2

nodes.name: N_s <= 2^k sqrt(N) via square-free parts
nodes.statement: Let us now look at \(N_s\). We write every \(n \leq N\) which has only small prime divisors in the form \(n = a_n b_n^2\), where \(a_n\) is the square-free part. Every \(a_n\) is thus a product of \emph{different} small primes, and we conclude that there are precisely \(2^k\) different square-free parts. Furthermore, as \(b_n^2 \leq n \leq N\), we find that there are at most \(\sqrt{N}\) different square parts, and so \[ N_s \leq 2^k \sqrt{N}. \]
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: N_s <= 2^k sqrt(N) via square-free parts

nodes.name: Choose N = 2^{2k+2} for the contradiction
nodes.statement: Since (2) holds for any \(N\), it remains to find a number \(N\) with \(2^k \sqrt{N} < \frac{N}{2}\), or \(2^{k+1} < \sqrt{N}\), and for this \(N = 2^{2k+2}\) will do.
nodes.section: 1 Six proofs of the infinity of primes
nodes.statement_short: Choose N = 2^{2k+2} for the contradiction

nodes.name: WLOG f is monotone
nodes.statement: We may assume that \(f(n)\) is monotonely increasing. Otherwise, replace \(f(n)\) by \(F(n) = \max_{i \leq n} f(i)\); you can easily check that with this \(F(n)\) the sequence \(S\) again satisfies the subexponential growth condition.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG f is monotone

nodes.name: Assume P_S finite and bound the exponents
nodes.statement: Let us suppose for a contradiction that \(\mathbb{P}_S = \{p_1, \dots, p_k\}\) is finite. For \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), let \[ s_n = \varepsilon_n p_1^{\alpha_1} \cdots p_k^{\alpha_k}, \quad \text{with } \varepsilon_n \in \{1, 0, -1\}, \alpha_i \ge 0, \] where the \(\alpha_i = \alpha_i(n)\) depend on \(n\). (For \(s_n = 0\) we can put \(\alpha_i = 0\) for all \(i\).) Then \[ 2^{\alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_k} \leq |s_n| \leq 2^{2^{f(n)}} \quad \text{for } s_n \ne 0, \] and thus by taking the binary logarithm \[ 0 \leq \alpha_i \leq \alpha_1 + \dots + \alpha_k \leq 2^{f(n)} \quad \text{for } 1 \leq i \leq k. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume P_S finite and bound the exponents

nodes.name: Upper estimate on distinct |s_n|
nodes.statement: Hence there are not more than \(2^{f(n)} + 1\) different possible values for each \(\alpha_i = \alpha_i(n)\). Since \(f\) is monotone, this gives a first estimate \[ \#\{\text{distinct } |s_n| \ne 0 \text{ for } n \leq N\} \leq (2^{f(N)} + 1)^k \leq 2^{(f(N)+1)k}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Upper estimate on distinct |s_n|

nodes.name: Lower estimate from almost injectivity
nodes.statement: On the other hand, since \(S\) is almost injective only \(c\) terms in the sequence can be equal to 0, and each nonzero absolute value can occur at most \(2c\) times, so we get the lower estimate \[ \#\{\text{distinct } |s_n| \ne 0 \text{ for } n \leq N\} \ge \frac{N-c}{2c}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Lower estimate from almost injectivity

nodes.name: Combine and take logarithms
nodes.statement: Altogether, this gives \[ \frac{N-c}{2c} \leq 2^{k(f(N)+1)}. \] Taking again the logarithm with base 2 on both sides, we obtain \[ \log_2(N-c) - \log_2(2c) \leq k(f(N)+1) \quad \text{for all } N. \]
nodes.statement_short: Combine and take logarithms

nodes.name: Contradiction for large N by subexponential growth
nodes.statement: This, however, is plainly false for large \(N\), as \(k\) and \(c\) are constants, so \(\frac{\log_2(N-c)}{\log_2 N}\) goes to 1 for \(N \to \infty\), while \(\frac{f(N)}{\log_2 N}\) goes to 0.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction for large N by subexponential growth

nodes.name: Plan: binom(2n,n) would be too small without primes in (n,2n]
nodes.statement: We will estimate the size of the binomial coefficient $\binom{2n}{n}$ carefully enough to see that if it didn't have any prime factors in the range \(n < p \le 2n\), then it would be ``too small.'' Our argument is in five steps.
nodes.statement_short: Plan: binom(2n,n) would be too small without primes in (n,2n]

nodes.name: Small n <= 511 via Landau's trick
nodes.statement: We first prove Bertrand's postulate for $n \le 511$. For this one does not need to check 511 cases: it suffices (this is ``Landau's trick'') to check that \[ 2,3,5,7,13,23,43,83,163,317,521 \] is a sequence of prime numbers, where each is smaller than twice the previous one. Hence every interval \(\{y : n < y \le 2n\}\), with $n \le 511$, contains one of these 11 primes.
nodes.statement_short: Small n <= 511 via Landau's trick

nodes.name: Prove prod_{p<=x} p <= 4^{x-1}
nodes.statement: Next we prove that \begin{equation} \prod_{p \le x} p \le 4^{x-1} \quad \text{for all real } x \ge 2, \end{equation} where our notation --- here and in the following --- is meant to imply that the product is taken over all prime numbers $p \le x$. The proof that we present for this fact uses induction on the number of these primes. It is not from Erdős' original paper, but it is also due to Erdős, and it is a true Book Proof. First we note that if \(q\) is the largest prime with \(q \le x\), then \[ \prod_{p \le x} p = \prod_{p \le q} p \quad \text{and} \quad 4^{q-1} \le 4^{x-1}. \] Thus it suffices to check \eqref{eq:prod_prime_le} for the case where $x=q$ is a prime number. For $q=2$ we get ``$2 \le 4$,'' so we proceed to consider odd primes $q = 2m + 1$. (Here we may assume, by induction, that \eqref{eq:prod_prime_le} is valid for all integers $x$ in the set $\{2, 3, \dots, 2m\}$.) For $q = 2m + 1$ we split the product and compute \[ \prod_{p \le 2m + 1} p = \prod_{p \le m + 1} p \cdot \prod_{m + 1 < p \le 2m + 1} p \le 4^m \binom{2m + 1}{m} \le 4^m 2^{2m} = 4^{2m}. \] All the pieces of this ``one-line computation'' are easy to see. In fact, \[ \prod_{p \le m + 1} p \le 4^m \] holds by induction. The inequality \[ \prod_{m + 1 < p \le 2m + 1} p \le \binom{2m + 1}{m} \] follows from the observation that $\binom{2m + 1}{m} = \frac{(2m + 1)!}{m! (m + 1)!}$ is an integer, where the primes that we consider all are factors of the numerator $(2m + 1)!$, but not of the denominator $m! (m + 1)!$. Finally \[ \binom{2m + 1}{m} \le 2^{2m} \] holds since \[ \binom{2m + 1}{m} \quad \text{and} \quad \binom{2m + 1}{m + 1} \] are two (equal!) summands that appear in \[ \sum_{k = 0}^{2m + 1} \binom{2m + 1}{k} = 2^{2m + 1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Prove prod_{p<=x} p <= 4^{x-1}

nodes.name: State the product bound and the induction plan
nodes.statement: Next we prove that \begin{equation} \prod_{p \le x} p \le 4^{x-1} \quad \text{for all real } x \ge 2, \end{equation} where our notation --- here and in the following --- is meant to imply that the product is taken over all prime numbers $p \le x$. The proof that we present for this fact uses induction on the number of these primes. It is not from Erdős' original paper, but it is also due to Erdős, and it is a true Book Proof.
nodes.statement_short: State the product bound and the induction plan

nodes.name: Reduce to x = q prime
nodes.statement: First we note that if \(q\) is the largest prime with \(q \le x\), then \[ \prod_{p \le x} p = \prod_{p \le q} p \quad \text{and} \quad 4^{q-1} \le 4^{x-1}. \] Thus it suffices to check \eqref{eq:prod_prime_le} for the case where $x=q$ is a prime number.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to x = q prime

nodes.name: Base case and induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: For $q=2$ we get ``$2 \le 4$,'' so we proceed to consider odd primes $q = 2m + 1$. (Here we may assume, by induction, that \eqref{eq:prod_prime_le} is valid for all integers $x$ in the set $\{2, 3, \dots, 2m\}$.)
nodes.statement_short: Base case and induction hypothesis

nodes.name: Split the product for q = 2m+1
nodes.statement: For $q = 2m + 1$ we split the product and compute \[ \prod_{p \le 2m + 1} p = \prod_{p \le m + 1} p \cdot \prod_{m + 1 < p \le 2m + 1} p \le 4^m \binom{2m + 1}{m} \le 4^m 2^{2m} = 4^{2m}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Split the product for q = 2m+1

nodes.name: Justify each inequality of the one-line computation
nodes.statement: All the pieces of this ``one-line computation'' are easy to see. In fact, \[ \prod_{p \le m + 1} p \le 4^m \] holds by induction. The inequality \[ \prod_{m + 1 < p \le 2m + 1} p \le \binom{2m + 1}{m} \] follows from the observation that $\binom{2m + 1}{m} = \frac{(2m + 1)!}{m! (m + 1)!}$ is an integer, where the primes that we consider all are factors of the numerator $(2m + 1)!$, but not of the denominator $m! (m + 1)!$. Finally \[ \binom{2m + 1}{m} \le 2^{2m} \] holds since \[ \binom{2m + 1}{m} \quad \text{and} \quad \binom{2m + 1}{m + 1} \] are two (equal!) summands that appear in \[ \sum_{k = 0}^{2m + 1} \binom{2m + 1}{k} = 2^{2m + 1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Justify each inequality of the one-line computation

nodes.name: Prime powers dividing binom(2n,n)
nodes.statement: From Legendre's theorem we get that $\binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{n! n!}$ contains the prime factor $p$ exactly \[ \sum_{k \geq 1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor \right) \] times. Here each summand is at most 1, since it satisfies \[ \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor < \frac{2n}{p^k} - 2 \left( \frac{n}{p^k} - 1 \right) = 2, \] and it is an integer. Furthermore the summands vanish whenever $p^k > 2n$. Thus $\binom{2n}{n}$ contains $p$ exactly \[ \sum_{k \geq 1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor \right) \le \max\{r : p^r \le 2n\} \] times. Hence the largest power of $p$ that divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ is not larger than $2n$. In particular, primes $p > \sqrt{2n}$ appear at most once in $\binom{2n}{n}$. Furthermore --- and this, according to Erdős, is the key fact for his proof --- primes $p$ that satisfy $\frac{2}{3} n < p < n$ do not divide $\binom{2n}{n}$ at all! Indeed, $3p > 2n$ implies (for $n \geq 3$, and hence $p \geq 3$) that $p$ and $2p$ are the only multiples of $p$ that appear as factors in the numerator of $\frac{(2n)!}{n! n!}$, while we get two $p$-factors in the denominator.
nodes.statement_short: Prime powers dividing binom(2n,n)

nodes.name: Legendre's formula: p-power in binom(2n,n) at most 2n
nodes.statement: From Legendre's theorem we get that $\binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{n! n!}$ contains the prime factor $p$ exactly \[ \sum_{k \geq 1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor \right) \] times. Here each summand is at most 1, since it satisfies \[ \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor < \frac{2n}{p^k} - 2 \left( \frac{n}{p^k} - 1 \right) = 2, \] and it is an integer. Furthermore the summands vanish whenever $p^k > 2n$. Thus $\binom{2n}{n}$ contains $p$ exactly \[ \sum_{k \geq 1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{2n}{p^k} \right\rfloor - 2 \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^k} \right\rfloor \right) \le \max\{r : p^r \le 2n\} \] times. Hence the largest power of $p$ that divides $\binom{2n}{n}$ is not larger than $2n$. In particular, primes $p > \sqrt{2n}$ appear at most once in $\binom{2n}{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: Legendre's formula: p-power in binom(2n,n) at most 2n

nodes.name: Primes in (2n/3, n) do not divide binom(2n,n)
nodes.statement: Furthermore --- and this, according to Erdős, is the key fact for his proof --- primes $p$ that satisfy $\frac{2}{3} n < p < n$ do not divide $\binom{2n}{n}$ at all! Indeed, $3p > 2n$ implies (for $n \geq 3$, and hence $p \geq 3$) that $p$ and $2p$ are the only multiples of $p$ that appear as factors in the numerator of $\frac{(2n)!}{n! n!}$, while we get two $p$-factors in the denominator.
nodes.statement_short: Primes in (2n/3, n) do not divide binom(2n,n)

nodes.name: Estimate binom(2n,n) from both sides
nodes.statement: Now we are ready to estimate \(\binom{2n}{n}\), benefitting from a suggestion by Raimund Seidel, which nicely improves Erdős' original argument. For \(n \ge 3\), using an estimate for the lower bound, we get \[ \frac{4^n}{2n} \le \binom{2n}{n} \le \prod_{p \le \sqrt{2n}} 2n \cdot \prod_{\sqrt{2n} < p \le \frac{2}{3}n} p \cdot \prod_{n < p \le 2n} p. \] Now, there are no more than \(\sqrt{2n}\) primes in the first factor; hence using (1) for the second factor and letting \(P(n)\) denote the number of primes between \(n\) and \(2n\) we get \[ \frac{4^n}{2n} < ((2n)^{\sqrt{2n}}) \cdot (4^{\frac{2}{3}n}) \cdot (2n)^{P(n)}, \] that is, \[ 4^{\frac{n}{3}} < (2n)^{\sqrt{2n}+1+P(n)}. \quad \text{(2)} \]
nodes.statement_short: Estimate binom(2n,n) from both sides

nodes.name: Factor binom(2n,n) over prime ranges
nodes.statement: Now we are ready to estimate \(\binom{2n}{n}\), benefitting from a suggestion by Raimund Seidel, which nicely improves Erdős' original argument. For \(n \ge 3\), using an estimate for the lower bound, we get \[ \frac{4^n}{2n} \le \binom{2n}{n} \le \prod_{p \le \sqrt{2n}} 2n \cdot \prod_{\sqrt{2n} < p \le \frac{2}{3}n} p \cdot \prod_{n < p \le 2n} p. \]
nodes.statement_short: Factor binom(2n,n) over prime ranges

nodes.name: Get 4^{n/3} < (2n)^{sqrt(2n)+1+P(n)}
nodes.statement: Now, there are no more than \(\sqrt{2n}\) primes in the first factor; hence using (1) for the second factor and letting \(P(n)\) denote the number of primes between \(n\) and \(2n\) we get \[ \frac{4^n}{2n} < ((2n)^{\sqrt{2n}}) \cdot (4^{\frac{2}{3}n}) \cdot (2n)^{P(n)}, \] that is, \[ 4^{\frac{n}{3}} < (2n)^{\sqrt{2n}+1+P(n)}. \quad \text{(2)} \]

nodes.name: Show P(n) > 0 for n >= 512
nodes.statement: Taking the logarithm to base 2, the last inequality is turned into \[ P(n) > \frac{2n}{3 \log_2(2n)} - (\sqrt{2n} + 1). \quad \text{(3)} \] It remains to verify that the right-hand side of (3) is positive for \(n\) large enough. We show that this is the case for \(n = 2^9 = 512\) (actually, it holds for \(n = 468\) onward). By writing \(2n - 1 = (\sqrt{2n} - 1)(\sqrt{2n} + 1)\) and cancelling the \((\sqrt{2n} + 1)\)-factor it suffices to show \[ \sqrt{2n}-1 > 3 \log_2(2n) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2^9. \quad \text{(4)} \] For \(n = 2^9\), (4) becomes \(31 > 30\), and comparing the derivatives \((\sqrt{x}-1)' = \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) and \((3 \log_2 x)' = \frac{3}{\log 2} \frac{1}{x}\) we see that \(\sqrt{x} - 1\) grows faster than \(3 \log_2 x\) for \(x > (\frac{6}{\log 2})^2 \approx 75\) and thus certainly for \(x \ge 2^{10} = 1024.\) \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Show P(n) > 0 for n >= 512

nodes.name: Logarithm gives lower bound on P(n)
nodes.statement: Taking the logarithm to base 2, the last inequality is turned into \[ P(n) > \frac{2n}{3 \log_2(2n)} - (\sqrt{2n} + 1). \quad \text{(3)} \]
nodes.statement_short: Logarithm gives lower bound on P(n)

nodes.name: Reduce to sqrt(2n) - 1 > 3 log_2(2n)
nodes.statement: It remains to verify that the right-hand side of (3) is positive for \(n\) large enough. We show that this is the case for \(n = 2^9 = 512\) (actually, it holds for \(n = 468\) onward). By writing \(2n - 1 = (\sqrt{2n} - 1)(\sqrt{2n} + 1)\) and cancelling the \((\sqrt{2n} + 1)\)-factor it suffices to show \[ \sqrt{2n}-1 > 3 \log_2(2n) \quad \text{for } n \ge 2^9. \quad \text{(4)} \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to sqrt(2n) - 1 > 3 log_2(2n)

nodes.name: Check at n = 2^9 and compare derivatives
nodes.statement: For \(n = 2^9\), (4) becomes \(31 > 30\), and comparing the derivatives \((\sqrt{x}-1)' = \frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\) and \((3 \log_2 x)' = \frac{3}{\log 2} \frac{1}{x}\) we see that \(\sqrt{x} - 1\) grows faster than \(3 \log_2 x\) for \(x > (\frac{6}{\log 2})^2 \approx 75\) and thus certainly for \(x \ge 2^{10} = 1024.\) \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Check at n = 2^9 and compare derivatives

nodes.name: Estimate sums by integrals
nodes.statement: There is a very simple-but-effective method of estimating sums by integrals.
nodes.statement_short: Estimate sums by integrals

nodes.name: Upper and lower rectangle comparisons with log n
nodes.statement: For estimating the harmonic numbers \[ H_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k} \] we draw the figure and derive from it \[ H_n - 1 = \sum_{k=2}^{n} \frac{1}{k} < \int_{1}^{n} \frac{1}{t} \, dt = \log n \] by comparing the area below the graph of $f(t) = \frac{1}{t} (1 \le t \le n)$ with the area of the dark shaded rectangles, and \[ H_n - \frac{1}{n} = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \frac{1}{k} > \int_{1}^{n} \frac{1}{t} \, dt = \log n \] by comparing with the area of the large rectangles (including the lightly shaded parts).
nodes.statement_short: Upper and lower rectangle comparisons with log n

nodes.name: Combine both estimates
nodes.statement: Taken together, this yields \[ \log n + \frac{1}{n} < H_n < \log n + 1. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Combine both estimates

nodes.name: Integral comparison for log n!
nodes.statement: The same method applied to \[ \log(n!) = \log 2 + \log 3 + \dots + \log n = \sum_{k=2}^{n} \log k \] yields \[ \log((n-1)!) < \int_{1}^{n} \log t \, dt < \log(n!), \] where the integral is easily computed: \[ \int_{1}^{n} \log t \, dt = \left[t\log t - t\right]_{1}^{n} = n\log n - n + 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Integral comparison for log n!

nodes.name: Exponentiate to get the bounds on n!
nodes.statement: Thus we get a lower estimate on $n!$ \[ n! > e^{n\log n - n + 1} = e\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n \] and at the same time an upper estimate \[ n! = n(n-1)! < n e^{n\log n - n + 1} = en\left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Exponentiate to get the bounds on n!

nodes.name: WLOG n >= 2k; assume binom(n,k) = m^l
nodes.statement: Note first that we may assume \(n \ge 2k\) because of \(\binom{n}{k} = \binom{n}{n-k}\). Suppose the theorem is false, and that \(\binom{n}{k} = m^\ell\). The proof, by contradiction, proceeds in the following four steps.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG n >= 2k; assume binom(n,k) = m^l

nodes.name: (1) Sylvester gives p^l | n - i, so n > k^2
nodes.statement: By Sylvester's theorem \ref{sylvester}, there is a prime factor \(p\) of \(\binom{n}{k}\) greater than \(k\), hence \(p^\ell\) divides \(n(n - 1) \dots (n - k + 1)\). Clearly, only one of the factors \(n - i\) can be a multiple of \(p\) (because \(p > k\)), and we conclude \(p^\ell \mid n - i\), and therefore \[ n \ge p^\ell > k^\ell \ge k^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: (1) Sylvester gives p^l | n - i, so n > k^2

nodes.name: (2) The parts a_j are distinct
nodes.statement: Consider any factor \(n - j\) of the numerator and write it in the form \(n - j = a_j m_j^\ell\), where \(a_j\) is not divisible by any nontrivial \(\ell\)-th power. We note by (1) that \(a_j\) has only prime divisors less than or equal to \(k\). We want to show next that \(a_i \ne a_j\) for \(i \ne j\). Assume to the contrary that \(a_i = a_j\) for some \(i < j\). Then \(m_i \ge m_j + 1\) and \begin{align*} k &> (n - i) - (n - j) = a_j(m_i^\ell - m_j^\ell) \ge a_j((m_j + 1)^\ell - m_j^\ell)\\ &> a_j \ell m_j^{\ell-1} \ge \ell (a_j m_j^\ell)^{1/2} \ge \ell (n - k + 1)^{1/2}\\ &\ge \ell \left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)^{1/2} > n^{1/2}, \end{align*} which contradicts \(n > k^2\) from above.
nodes.statement_short: (2) The parts a_j are distinct

nodes.name: Write n - j = a_j m_j^l
nodes.statement: Consider any factor \(n - j\) of the numerator and write it in the form \(n - j = a_j m_j^\ell\), where \(a_j\) is not divisible by any nontrivial \(\ell\)-th power. We note by (1) that \(a_j\) has only prime divisors less than or equal to \(k\).
nodes.statement_short: Write n - j = a_j m_j^l

nodes.name: a_i = a_j leads to a contradiction with n > k^2
nodes.statement: We want to show next that \(a_i \ne a_j\) for \(i \ne j\). Assume to the contrary that \(a_i = a_j\) for some \(i < j\). Then \(m_i \ge m_j + 1\) and \begin{align*} k &> (n - i) - (n - j) = a_j(m_i^\ell - m_j^\ell) \ge a_j((m_j + 1)^\ell - m_j^\ell)\\ &> a_j \ell m_j^{\ell-1} \ge \ell (a_j m_j^\ell)^{1/2} \ge \ell (n - k + 1)^{1/2}\\ &\ge \ell \left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)^{1/2} > n^{1/2}, \end{align*} which contradicts \(n > k^2\) from above.
nodes.statement_short: a_i = a_j leads to a contradiction with n > k^2

nodes.name: (3) The a_i are exactly 1..k
nodes.statement: Next we prove that the \(a_i\)'s are the integers \(1, 2, \dots, k\) in some order. (According to Erdős, this is the crux of the proof.) Since we already know that they are all distinct, it suffices to prove that \[ a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} \text{ divides } k!. \] Substituting \(n - j = a_j m_j^\ell\) into the equation \(\binom{n}{k} = m^\ell\), we obtain \[ a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} (m_0 m_1 \cdots m_{k-1})^\ell = k! m^\ell. \] Canceling the common factors of \(m_0 \cdots m_{k-1}\) and \(m\) yields \[ a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1} u^\ell = k! v^\ell \] with \(\gcd(u, v) = 1\). It remains to show that \(v = 1\). If not, then \(v\) contains a prime divisor \(p\). Since \(\gcd(u, v) = 1\), \(p\) must be a prime divisor of \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1}\) and hence is less than or equal to \(k\). By the theorem of Legendre, we know that \(k!\) contains \(p\) to the power \(\sum_{i \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor\). We now estimate the exponent of \(p\) in \(n(n - 1) \dots (n - k + 1)\). Let \(i\) be a positive integer, and let \(b_1 < b_2 < \dots < b_s\) be the multiples of \(p^i\) among \(n, n - 1, \dots, n - k + 1\). Then \(b_s = b_1 + (s - 1)p^i\) and hence \[ (s - 1)p^i = b_s - b_1 \le n - (n - k + 1) = k - 1, \] which implies \[ s \le \left\lfloor \frac{k - 1}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \le \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1. \] So for each \(i\), the number of multiples of \(p^i\) among \(n, \dots, n-k+1\), and hence among the \(a_j\)'s, is bounded by \(\left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1\). This implies that the exponent of \(p\) in \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1}\) is at most \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \] with the reasoning that we used for Legendre's theorem in Chapter 2. The only difference is that this time the sum stops at \(i = \ell - 1\), since the \(a_j\)'s contain no \(\ell\)-th powers. Taking both counts together, we find that the exponent of \(p\) in \(v^\ell\) is at most \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) - \sum_{i \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor \le \ell - 1, \] and we have our desired contradiction, since \(v^\ell\) is an \(\ell\)-th power. This suffices already to settle the case \(\ell = 2\). Indeed, since \(k \ge 4\), one of the \(a_i\)'s must be equal to 4, but the \(a_i\)'s contain no squares. So let us now assume that \(\ell \ge 3\).
nodes.statement_short: (3) The a_i are exactly 1..k

nodes.name: Reduce to a_0...a_{k-1} | k!
nodes.statement: Next we prove that the \(a_i\)'s are the integers \(1, 2, \dots, k\) in some order. (According to Erdős, this is the crux of the proof.) Since we already know that they are all distinct, it suffices to prove that \[ a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} \text{ divides } k!. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a_0...a_{k-1} | k!

nodes.name: Obtain a_0...a_{k-1} u^l = k! v^l with gcd(u,v) = 1
nodes.statement: Substituting \(n - j = a_j m_j^\ell\) into the equation \(\binom{n}{k} = m^\ell\), we obtain \[ a_0 a_1 \cdots a_{k-1} (m_0 m_1 \cdots m_{k-1})^\ell = k! m^\ell. \] Canceling the common factors of \(m_0 \cdots m_{k-1}\) and \(m\) yields \[ a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1} u^\ell = k! v^\ell \] with \(\gcd(u, v) = 1\).
nodes.statement_short: Obtain a_0...a_{k-1} u^l = k! v^l with gcd(u,v) = 1

nodes.name: Take a prime p | v, so p <= k
nodes.statement: It remains to show that \(v = 1\). If not, then \(v\) contains a prime divisor \(p\). Since \(\gcd(u, v) = 1\), \(p\) must be a prime divisor of \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1}\) and hence is less than or equal to \(k\).
nodes.statement_short: Take a prime p | v, so p <= k

nodes.name: Legendre's count of p in k!
nodes.statement: By the theorem of Legendre, we know that \(k!\) contains \(p\) to the power \(\sum_{i \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor\). We now estimate the exponent of \(p\) in \(n(n - 1) \dots (n - k + 1)\).
nodes.statement_short: Legendre's count of p in k!

nodes.name: Count multiples of p^i among n..n-k+1
nodes.statement: Let \(i\) be a positive integer, and let \(b_1 < b_2 < \dots < b_s\) be the multiples of \(p^i\) among \(n, n - 1, \dots, n - k + 1\). Then \(b_s = b_1 + (s - 1)p^i\) and hence \[ (s - 1)p^i = b_s - b_1 \le n - (n - k + 1) = k - 1, \] which implies \[ s \le \left\lfloor \frac{k - 1}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \le \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1. \] So for each \(i\), the number of multiples of \(p^i\) among \(n, \dots, n-k+1\), and hence among the \(a_j\)'s, is bounded by \(\left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1\). This implies that the exponent of \(p\) in \(a_0 a_1 \dots a_{k-1}\) is at most \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) \] with the reasoning that we used for Legendre's theorem in Chapter 2. The only difference is that this time the sum stops at \(i = \ell - 1\), since the \(a_j\)'s contain no \(\ell\)-th powers.
nodes.statement_short: Count multiples of p^i among n..n-k+1

nodes.name: Exponent of p in v^l is < l: contradiction
nodes.statement: Taking both counts together, we find that the exponent of \(p\) in \(v^\ell\) is at most \[ \sum_{i=1}^{\ell-1} \left( \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor + 1 \right) - \sum_{i \ge 1} \left\lfloor \frac{k}{p^i} \right\rfloor \le \ell - 1, \] and we have our desired contradiction, since \(v^\ell\) is an \(\ell\)-th power.
nodes.statement_short: Exponent of p in v^l is < l: contradiction

nodes.name: Settles l = 2; assume l >= 3
nodes.statement: This suffices already to settle the case \(\ell = 2\). Indeed, since \(k \ge 4\), one of the \(a_i\)'s must be equal to 4, but the \(a_i\)'s contain no squares. So let us now assume that \(\ell \ge 3\).
nodes.statement_short: Settles l = 2; assume l >= 3

nodes.name: (4) Final chain of inequalities for l >= 3
nodes.statement: Since \(k \ge 4\), we must have \(a_{i_1} = 1\), \(a_{i_2} = 2\), \(a_{i_3} = 4\) for some \(i_1, i_2, i_3\), that is, \[ n - i_1 = m_1^\ell, \quad n - i_2 = 2m_2^\ell, \quad n - i_3 = 4m_3^\ell. \] We claim that \((n - i_2)^2 \ne (n - i_1)(n - i_3)\). If not, put \(b = n - i_2\) and \(n - i_1 = b - x, n - i_3 = b + y\), where \(0 < |x|, |y| < k\). Hence \[ b^2 = (b - x)(b + y) \quad \text{or} \quad (y - x)b = xy, \] where \(x = y\) is plainly impossible. Now we have by part (1) \[ |xy| = b |y - x| \ge b > n - k > (k - 1)^2 \ge |xy|, \] which is absurd. So we have \(m_2^2 \ne m_1 m_3\), where we assume \(m_2^2 > m_1 m_3\) (the other case being analogous), and proceed to our last chain of inequalities. We obtain \begin{align*} 2(k - 1)n & > n^2 - (n - k + 1)^2 > (n - i_2)^2 - (n - i_1)(n - i_3)\\ & = 4[m_2^{2\ell} - (m_1 m_3)^\ell] \ge 4[(m_1 m_3 + 1)^\ell - (m_1 m_3)^\ell] \\ & \ge 4 \ell m_1^{\ell-1} m_3^{\ell-1}. \end{align*} Since \(\ell \ge 3\) and \(n > k^\ell \ge k^3 > 6k\), this yields \begin{align*} 2(k - 1)n m_1 m_3 & > 4 \ell m_1^\ell m_3^\ell = \ell (n - i_1)(n - i_3) \\ & > \ell (n - k + 1)^2 > 3 \left(n - \frac{n}{6}\right)^2 > 2n^2. \end{align*} Now since \(m_i \le n^{1/\ell} \le n ^{1/3}\) we finally obtain \[ kn^{2/3} \ge km_1m_3 > (k - 1)m_1m_3 > n, \] or \(k^3 > n\). With this contradiction, the proof is complete. \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: (4) Final chain of inequalities for l >= 3

nodes.name: a_{i1} = 1, a_{i2} = 2, a_{i3} = 4
nodes.statement: Since \(k \ge 4\), we must have \(a_{i_1} = 1\), \(a_{i_2} = 2\), \(a_{i_3} = 4\) for some \(i_1, i_2, i_3\), that is, \[ n - i_1 = m_1^\ell, \quad n - i_2 = 2m_2^\ell, \quad n - i_3 = 4m_3^\ell. \]

nodes.name: (n-i_2)^2 differs from (n-i_1)(n-i_3)
nodes.statement: We claim that \((n - i_2)^2 \ne (n - i_1)(n - i_3)\). If not, put \(b = n - i_2\) and \(n - i_1 = b - x, n - i_3 = b + y\), where \(0 < |x|, |y| < k\). Hence \[ b^2 = (b - x)(b + y) \quad \text{or} \quad (y - x)b = xy, \] where \(x = y\) is plainly impossible. Now we have by part (1) \[ |xy| = b |y - x| \ge b > n - k > (k - 1)^2 \ge |xy|, \] which is absurd.
nodes.statement_short: (n-i_2)^2 differs from (n-i_1)(n-i_3)

nodes.name: Chain of inequalities
nodes.statement: So we have \(m_2^2 \ne m_1 m_3\), where we assume \(m_2^2 > m_1 m_3\) (the other case being analogous), and proceed to our last chain of inequalities. We obtain \begin{align*} 2(k - 1)n & > n^2 - (n - k + 1)^2 > (n - i_2)^2 - (n - i_1)(n - i_3)\\ & = 4[m_2^{2\ell} - (m_1 m_3)^\ell] \ge 4[(m_1 m_3 + 1)^\ell - (m_1 m_3)^\ell] \\ & \ge 4 \ell m_1^{\ell-1} m_3^{\ell-1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Chain of inequalities

nodes.name: Use l >= 3 and n > 6k
nodes.statement: Since \(\ell \ge 3\) and \(n > k^\ell \ge k^3 > 6k\), this yields \begin{align*} 2(k - 1)n m_1 m_3 & > 4 \ell m_1^\ell m_3^\ell = \ell (n - i_1)(n - i_3) \\ & > \ell (n - k + 1)^2 > 3 \left(n - \frac{n}{6}\right)^2 > 2n^2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Use l >= 3 and n > 6k

nodes.name: Get k^3 > n, contradiction
nodes.statement: Now since \(m_i \le n^{1/\ell} \le n ^{1/3}\) we finally obtain \[ kn^{2/3} \ge km_1m_3 > (k - 1)m_1m_3 > n, \] or \(k^3 > n\). With this contradiction, the proof is complete. \qedhere
nodes.statement_short: Get k^3 > n, contradiction

nodes.name: Case p = 2
nodes.statement: For $p = 2$ take $s = 1$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Case p = 2

nodes.name: Equivalence relation by additive and multiplicative inverses
nodes.statement: For odd $p$, we construct the equivalence relation on $\{1, 2, \dots, p - 1\}$ that is generated by identifying every element with its additive inverse and with its multiplicative inverse in $\mathbb{Z}_p$. Thus the ``general'' equivalence classes will contain four elements \[ \{x, -x, \overline{x}, -\overline{x}\} \] since such a 4-element set contains both inverses for all its elements. However, there are smaller equivalence classes if some of the four numbers are not distinct:
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Equivalence relation by additive and multiplicative inverses

nodes.name: x = -x impossible
nodes.statement: $x \equiv -x$ is impossible for odd $p$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: x = -x impossible

nodes.name: x = x̄ gives the class {1, p-1}
nodes.statement: $x \equiv \overline{x}$ is equivalent to $x^2 \equiv 1$. This has two solutions, namely $x = 1$ and $x = p - 1$, leading to the equivalence class $\{1, p - 1\}$ of size 2.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: x = x̄ gives the class {1, p-1}

nodes.name: x = -x̄ gives solutions of x^2 = -1
nodes.statement: $x \equiv -\overline{x}$ is equivalent to $x^2 \equiv -1$. This equation may have no solution or two distinct solutions $x_0, p - x_0$: in this case the equivalence class is $\{x_0, p - x_0\}$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: x = -x̄ gives solutions of x^2 = -1

nodes.name: p = 4m+3: no second pair, no solution
nodes.statement: The set $\{1, 2, \dots, p - 1\}$ has $p - 1$ elements, and we have partitioned it into quadruples (equivalence classes of size 4), plus one or two pairs (equivalence classes of size 2). For $p - 1 = 4m + 2$ we find that there is only the one pair $\{1, p - 1\}$, the rest is quadruples, and thus $s^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ has no solution.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: p = 4m+3: no second pair, no solution

nodes.name: p = 4m+1: second pair gives two solutions
nodes.statement: For $p - 1 = 4m$ there has to be the second pair, and this contains the two solutions of $s^2 \equiv -1$ that we were looking for.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: p = 4m+1: second pair gives two solutions

nodes.name: Consider (floor(sqrt p)+1)^2 pairs
nodes.statement: Consider the pairs $(x', y')$ of integers with $0 \leq x', y' \leq \sqrt{p}$, that is, $x', y' \in \{0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor\}$. There are $(\lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor + 1)^2$ such pairs.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Consider (floor(sqrt p)+1)^2 pairs

nodes.name: More than p pairs: two agree mod p
nodes.statement: Using the estimate $\lfloor x \rfloor + 1 > x$ for $x = \sqrt{p}$, we see that we have more than $p$ such pairs of integers. Thus for any $s \in \mathbb{Z}$, it is impossible that all the values $x' - sy'$ produced by the pairs $(x', y')$ are distinct modulo $p$. That is, for every $s$ there are two distinct pairs \[ (x', y'), (x'', y'') \in \{0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor\}^2 \] with $x' - sy' \equiv x'' - sy'' \pmod{p}$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: More than p pairs: two agree mod p

nodes.name: Differences give x = ±sy mod p, not both zero
nodes.statement: Now we take differences: We have $x' - x'' \equiv s(y' - y'') \pmod{p}$. Thus if we define $x := |x' - x''|$, $y := |y' - y''|$, then we get \[ (x, y) \in \{0, 1, \dots, \lfloor \sqrt{p} \rfloor\}^2 \quad \text{with} \quad x \equiv \pm sy \pmod{p}. \] Also we know that not both $x$ and $y$ can be zero, because the pairs $(x', y')$ and $(x'', y'')$ are distinct.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Differences give x = ±sy mod p, not both zero

nodes.name: With s^2 = -1 from Lemma 1, x^2 + y^2 is in (0, 2p) and divisible by p
nodes.statement: Now let $s$ be a solution of $s^2 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$, which exists by Lemma 1. Then $x^2 \equiv s^2 y^2 = -y^2 \pmod{p}$, and so we have produced \[ (x, y) \in \mathbb{Z}^2 \quad \text{with} \quad 0 < x^2 + y^2 < 2p \quad \text{and} \quad x^2 + y^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}. \]
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: With s^2 = -1 from Lemma 1, x^2 + y^2 is in (0, 2p) and divisible by p

nodes.name: Hence x^2 + y^2 = p
nodes.statement: But $p$ is the only number between $0$ and $2p$ that is divisible by $p$. Thus $x^2 + y^2 = p$: done!
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Hence x^2 + y^2 = p

nodes.name: The finite set S of solutions of 4xy + z^2 = p
nodes.statement: We study the set \[ S := \{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{Z}^3 : 4xy + z^2 = p, \ x > 0, \ y > 0\}. \] This set is finite. Indeed, $x \geq 1$ and $y \geq 1$ implies $y \leq \frac{p}{4}$ and $x \leq \frac{p}{4}$. So there are only finitely many possible values for $x$ and $y$, and given $x$ and $y$, there are at most two values for $z$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: The finite set S of solutions of 4xy + z^2 = p

nodes.name: First involution: |T| = |U|
nodes.statement: The first linear involution is given by \[ f : S \to S, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (y, x, -z), \] that is, ``interchange $x$ and $y$, and negate $z$.'' This clearly maps $S$ to itself, and it is an \emph{involution}: Applied twice, it yields the identity. Also, $f$ has no fixed points, since $z = 0$ would imply $p = 4xy$, which is impossible. Furthermore, $f$ maps the solutions in \[ T := \{(x, y, z) \in S : z > 0\} \] to the solutions in $S \setminus T$, which satisfy $z < 0$. Also, $f$ reverses the signs of $x - y$ and of $z$, so it maps the solutions in \[ U := \{(x, y, z) \in S : (x - y) + z > 0\} \] to the solutions in $S \setminus U$. For this we have to see that there is no solution with $(x - y) + z = 0$, but there is none since this would give $p = 4xy + z^2 = 4xy + (x - y)^2 = (x + y)^2$. What do we get from the study of $f$? The main observation is that since $f$ maps the sets $T$ and $U$ to their complements, it also interchanges the elements in $T \setminus U$ with these in $U \setminus T$. That is, there is the same number of solutions in $U$ that are not in $T$ as there are solutions in $T$ that are not in $U$ --- \emph{so $T$ and $U$ have the same cardinality}.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: First involution: |T| = |U|

nodes.name: f swaps x, y and negates z
nodes.statement: The first linear involution is given by \[ f : S \to S, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (y, x, -z), \] that is, ``interchange $x$ and $y$, and negate $z$.'' This clearly maps $S$ to itself, and it is an \emph{involution}: Applied twice, it yields the identity.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: f swaps x, y and negates z

nodes.name: f maps T and U to their complements
nodes.statement: Also, $f$ has no fixed points, since $z = 0$ would imply $p = 4xy$, which is impossible. Furthermore, $f$ maps the solutions in \[ T := \{(x, y, z) \in S : z > 0\} \] to the solutions in $S \setminus T$, which satisfy $z < 0$. Also, $f$ reverses the signs of $x - y$ and of $z$, so it maps the solutions in \[ U := \{(x, y, z) \in S : (x - y) + z > 0\} \] to the solutions in $S \setminus U$. For this we have to see that there is no solution with $(x - y) + z = 0$, but there is none since this would give $p = 4xy + z^2 = 4xy + (x - y)^2 = (x + y)^2$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: f maps T and U to their complements

nodes.name: T and U have the same cardinality
nodes.statement: What do we get from the study of $f$? The main observation is that since $f$ maps the sets $T$ and $U$ to their complements, it also interchanges the elements in $T \setminus U$ with these in $U \setminus T$. That is, there is the same number of solutions in $U$ that are not in $T$ as there are solutions in $T$ that are not in $U$ --- \emph{so $T$ and $U$ have the same cardinality}.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: T and U have the same cardinality

nodes.name: Second involution: |U| is odd
nodes.statement: The second involution that we study is an involution on the set $U$: \[ g : U \to U, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (x - y + z, y, 2y - z). \] First we check that indeed this is a well-defined map: If $(x, y, z) \in U$, then $x - y + z > 0$, $y > 0$ and $4(x - y + z)y + (2y - z)^2 = 4xy + z^2$, so $g(x, y, z) \in S$. By $(x - y + z) - y + (2y - z) = x > 0$ we find that indeed $g(x, y, z) \in U$. Also $g$ is an involution: $g(x, y, z) = (x - y + z, y, 2y - z)$ is mapped by $g$ to $((x - y + z) - y + (2y - z), y, 2y - (2y - z)) = (x, y, z)$. And finally $g$ has exactly one fixed point: \[ (x, y, z) = g(x, y, z) = (x - y + z, y, 2y - z) \] implies that $y = z$, but then $p = 4xy + y^2 = (4x + y)y$, which holds only for $y = z = 1$ and $x = \frac{p - 1}{4}$. But if $g$ is an involution on $U$ that has exactly one fixed point, then \emph{the cardinality of $U$ is odd.}
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Second involution: |U| is odd

nodes.name: g is well defined on U
nodes.statement: The second involution that we study is an involution on the set $U$: \[ g : U \to U, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (x - y + z, y, 2y - z). \] First we check that indeed this is a well-defined map: If $(x, y, z) \in U$, then $x - y + z > 0$, $y > 0$ and $4(x - y + z)y + (2y - z)^2 = 4xy + z^2$, so $g(x, y, z) \in S$. By $(x - y + z) - y + (2y - z) = x > 0$ we find that indeed $g(x, y, z) \in U$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: g is well defined on U

nodes.name: g is an involution
nodes.statement: Also $g$ is an involution: $g(x, y, z) = (x - y + z, y, 2y - z)$ is mapped by $g$ to $((x - y + z) - y + (2y - z), y, 2y - (2y - z)) = (x, y, z)$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: g is an involution

nodes.name: g has exactly one fixed point
nodes.statement: And finally $g$ has exactly one fixed point: \[ (x, y, z) = g(x, y, z) = (x - y + z, y, 2y - z) \] implies that $y = z$, but then $p = 4xy + y^2 = (4x + y)y$, which holds only for $y = z = 1$ and $x = \frac{p - 1}{4}$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: g has exactly one fixed point

nodes.name: |U| is odd
nodes.statement: But if $g$ is an involution on $U$ that has exactly one fixed point, then \emph{the cardinality of $U$ is odd.}
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: |U| is odd

nodes.name: Third involution has a fixed point
nodes.statement: The third, trivial, involution that we study is the involution on $T$ that interchanges $x$ and $y$: \[ h : T \to T, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (y, x, z). \] This map is clearly well-defined, and an involution. We combine now our knowledge derived from the other two involutions: The cardinality of $T$ is equal to the cardinality of $U$, which is odd. But if $h$ is an involution on a finite set of odd cardinality, then it \emph{has a fixed point}: There is a point $(x, y, z) \in T$ with $x = y$, that is, a solution of \[ p = 4x^2 + z^2 = (2x)^2 + z^2. \]
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Third involution has a fixed point

nodes.name: h swaps x and y on T
nodes.statement: The third, trivial, involution that we study is the involution on $T$ that interchanges $x$ and $y$: \[ h : T \to T, \quad (x, y, z) \mapsto (y, x, z). \] This map is clearly well-defined, and an involution.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: h swaps x and y on T

nodes.name: |T| odd forces a fixed point x = y, so p = (2x)^2 + z^2
nodes.statement: We combine now our knowledge derived from the other two involutions: The cardinality of $T$ is equal to the cardinality of $U$, which is odd. But if $h$ is an involution on a finite set of odd cardinality, then it \emph{has a fixed point}: There is a point $(x, y, z) \in T$ with $x = y$, that is, a solution of \[ p = 4x^2 + z^2 = (2x)^2 + z^2. \]
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: |T| odd forces a fixed point x = y, so p = (2x)^2 + z^2

nodes.name: Solutions of 4xy + z^2 = p as winged squares
nodes.statement: Again we fix a prime number $p = 4n + 1$ and consider the set of solutions \[ T = \{(x, y, z) \in \mathbb{N}^3 : 4xy + z^2 = p\}. \] Each element of this set gives rise to a \emph{winged square}: This is the figure consisting of a square and four rectangles in the plane that you get if you start with a square of side length $z$ and at each vertex attach a rectangle of side-lengths $x$ and $y$ in a rotation-symmetric way, such that the edge of length $x$ points away from the square, while the edge of length $y$ runs along the side of the square.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Solutions of 4xy + z^2 = p as winged squares

nodes.name: Normalize winged squares up to congruence
nodes.statement: We consider two winged squares ``the same'' if they are congruent. One way to make this unique, such that the representation of the winged square depends only on its boundary curve, is to require that the L formed by the two edges in the upper right-hand corner is at least as high as it is wide. If this condition is not satisfied, then a mirror image (reflected, e.g., in a vertical axis), will repair this. So each solution in $T$ corresponds to a \emph{unique} winged square of area $4xy + z^2 = p$, and indeed this is reversible: From each winged square we can read off a solution.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Normalize winged squares up to congruence

nodes.name: Winged shapes
nodes.statement: Taking the union of the square and the four rectangles, we get for each winged square what we will call a \emph{unique winged shape}: This is a polyomino of area $p$ with four-fold rotation symmetry, which has twelve vertices: eight convex ones with inner right angle and four non-convex ones with outer right angle. (We can't get a square shape, since $p$ is a prime, so it can't be a square number.) Again we will consider winged shapes ``the same'' if they are congruent, so we might assume that the L shape in the upper right-hand corner is at least as high as it is wide.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Winged shapes

nodes.name: Exactly one shape gives a single square, so |T| is odd
nodes.statement: Now we are getting very close to the punch line: For each winged shape we get \emph{either one or two} winged squares, by simultaneously drawing, in a rotation-symmetric way, vertical and horizontal lines to the interior starting at the non-convex vertices. We get \emph{only one} solution if the shape has the symmetry of a square, that is, if the two arms of the L shapes have the same length. This happens exactly if $y = z$, but then $p = 4xz + z^2 = (4x + z)z$; assuming that $p$ is a prime, this implies that $z = 1$ and $x = n$. In other words: Exactly one winged shape yields a single winged square, while all other winged shapes yield two winged squares each. Consequently, \emph{the number $|T|$ of winged squares is odd.}
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Exactly one shape gives a single square, so |T| is odd

nodes.name: Flip pairs leave an odd number with x = y
nodes.statement: However, the winged squares with non-square rectangles (with $x \neq y$) come in pairs, as we can always flip the four rectangular wings between vertical and horizontal format (that is, exchange $x$ and $y$). As $|T|$ is odd, this implies that there is an odd number of winged squares whose wings are squares, that is, $T$ contains an odd number of triples $(x, y, z)$ with $x = y$, and hence at least one, and this yields a solution to $(2x)^2 + z^2 = p$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Flip pairs leave an odd number with x = y

nodes.name: Define representable; theorem follows from five facts
nodes.statement: Call a number $n$ \textit{representable} if it is a sum of two squares, that is, if $n = x^2 + y^2$ for some $x, y \in \mathbb{N}_0$. The theorem is a consequence of the following five facts.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: Define representable; theorem follows from five facts

nodes.name: (1) 1, 2 and primes 4m+1 are representable
nodes.statement: $1 = 1^2 + 0^2$ and $2 = 1^2 + 1^2$ are representable. Every prime of the form $p = 4m + 1$ is representable.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: (1) 1, 2 and primes 4m+1 are representable

nodes.name: (2) Products of representable numbers
nodes.statement: The product of any two representable numbers $n_1 = x_1^2 + y_1^2$ and $n_2 = x_2^2 + y_2^2$ is representable: $n_1 n_2 = (x_1 x_2 + y_1 y_2)^2 + (x_1 y_2 - x_2 y_1)^2$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: (2) Products of representable numbers

nodes.name: (3) Square multiples
nodes.statement: If $n$ is representable, $n = x^2 + y^2$, then also $nz^2$ is representable, by $nz^2 = (xz)^2 + (yz)^2$.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: (3) Square multiples

nodes.name: The if part
nodes.statement: Facts (1), (2) and (3) together yield the ``if'' part of the theorem.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: The if part

nodes.name: (4) p = 4m+3 dividing x^2+y^2 divides x and y
nodes.statement: If $p = 4m + 3$ is a prime that divides a representable number $n = x^2 + y^2$, then $p$ divides both $x$ and $y$, and thus $p^2$ divides $n$. In fact, if we had $x \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, then we could find $\overline{x}$ such that $x\overline{x} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$, multiply the equation $x^2 + y^2 \equiv 0$ by $\overline{x}^2$, and thus we would obtain that $1 + y^2 \overline{x}^2 = 1 + \left(\overline{x} y\right)^2 \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, which is impossible for $p = 4m + 3$ by Lemma 1.
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: (4) p = 4m+3 dividing x^2+y^2 divides x and y

nodes.name: (5) Strip p^2; the only-if part
nodes.statement: If $n$ is representable, and $p = 4m + 3$ divides $n$, then $p^2$ divides $n$, and $n/p^2$ is representable. This follows from (4), and completes the proof. \qedhere
nodes.section: 4 Representing numbers as sums of two squares
nodes.statement_short: (5) Strip p^2; the only-if part

nodes.name: Factor x^{p-1} - 1 using Fermat
nodes.statement: From Fermat's little theorem, the polynomial $x^{p-1} - 1 \in \mathbb{Z}_p[x]$ has as roots all nonzero residues. Next we note that \[ x^{p-1} - 1 = \left(x^{\frac{p-1}{2}} - 1\right)\left(x^{\frac{p-1}{2}} + 1\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Factor x^{p-1} - 1 using Fermat

nodes.name: Residues are roots of the first factor, nonresidues of the second
nodes.statement: Suppose $a \equiv b^2 \pmod{p}$ is a quadratic residue. Then by Fermat's little theorem $a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv b^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$. Hence the quadratic residues are precisely the roots of the first factor $x^{\frac{p-1}{2}} - 1$, and the $\frac{p-1}{2}$ nonresidues must thus be the roots of the second factor $x^{\frac{p-1}{2}} + 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Residues are roots of the first factor, nonresidues of the second

nodes.name: Compare with the Legendre symbol
nodes.statement: Comparing this to the definition of the Legendre symbol, we obtain \[ (\frac{a}{p}) \equiv a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \pmod{p}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Compare with the Legendre symbol

nodes.name: -u_i never equals v_j
nodes.statement: Suppose $u_1, \dots, u_s$ are the residues smaller than $0$, and that $v_1, \dots, v_{\frac{p-1}{2} - s}$ are those greater than $0$. If $-u_i = v_j$, then $u_i + v_j \equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. Now $u_i \equiv ka, v_j \equiv \ell a \pmod{p}$ implies $p \mid (k + \ell) a$. As $p$ and $a$ are relatively prime, $p$ must divide $k + \ell$ which is impossible, since $k + \ell \le p-1$.
nodes.statement_short: -u_i never equals v_j

nodes.name: Product identity for the residues
nodes.statement: Thus the numbers $-u_1, \dots, -u_s$ are between $1$ and $\frac{p-1}{2}$, and are all different from the $v_j$'s; hence $\{-u_1, \dots, -u_s, v_1, \dots, v_{\frac{p-1}{2} - s}\} = \{1, 2, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2}\}$. Therefore \[ \prod_{i} (-u_i) \prod_{j} v_j = \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!, \] which implies \[ (-1)^s \prod_{i} u_i \prod_{j} v_j \equiv \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)! \pmod{p}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Product identity for the residues

nodes.name: Residues of 1a..(p-1)a/2 give a^{(p-1)/2}
nodes.statement: Now remember how we obtained the numbers $u_i$ and $v_j$; they are the residues of $1a, \dots, \frac{p-1}{2}a$. Hence \[ \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)! \equiv (-1)^s \prod_{i} u_i \prod_{j} v_j \equiv (-1)^s \left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)! a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \pmod{p}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Residues of 1a..(p-1)a/2 give a^{(p-1)/2}

nodes.name: Cancel and apply Euler's criterion
nodes.statement: Cancelling $\left(\frac{p-1}{2}\right)!$ together with Euler's criterion gives \[ (\frac{a}{p}) \equiv a^{\frac{p-1}{2}} \equiv (-1)^s \pmod{p}, \] and therefore $(\frac{a}{p}) = (-1)^s$, since $p$ is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Cancel and apply Euler's criterion

nodes.name: Lattice-point interpretation via Gauss' lemma
nodes.statement: The key to our first proof is a counting formula given by Lemma of Gauss. Let $p$ and $q$ be odd primes, and consider $(\frac{q}{p})$. Suppose $iq$ is a multiple of $q$ that reduces to negative residue $r_i < 0$ in the Lemma of Gauss. This means that there is a unique integer $j$ such that $-\frac{p}{2} < iq-jp < 0$. Note that $0 < j < \frac{q}{2}$ since $0 < i < \frac{p}{2}$. In other words, $(\frac{q}{p}) = (-1)^s$, where $s$ is the number of lattice points $(x, y)$, that is, pairs of integers $x$, $y$ satisfying \begin{equation} 0 < py - qx < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < x < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < y < \frac{q}{2}. \end{equation} Similarly, $(\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^t$ where $t$ is the number of lattice points $(x, y)$ with \begin{equation} 0 < qx - py < \frac{q}{2}, \quad 0 < x < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < y < \frac{q}{2}. \end{equation} Now look at the rectangle with side lengths $\frac{p}{2}$, $\frac{q}{2}$, and draw the two lines parallel to the diagonal $py = qx$, $y = \frac{q}{p}x + \frac{1}{2}$ or $py - qx = \frac{p}{2}$, respectively, $y = \frac{q}{p} \left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)$ or $qx - py = \frac{q}{2}$. The proof is now quickly completed by the following three observations:
nodes.statement_short: Lattice-point interpretation via Gauss' lemma

nodes.name: Count s via Gauss' lemma
nodes.statement: The key to our first proof is a counting formula given by Lemma of Gauss. Let $p$ and $q$ be odd primes, and consider $(\frac{q}{p})$.
nodes.statement_short: Count s via Gauss' lemma

nodes.name: (q/p) = (-1)^s, s lattice points in a strip
nodes.statement: Suppose $iq$ is a multiple of $q$ that reduces to negative residue $r_i < 0$ in the Lemma of Gauss. This means that there is a unique integer $j$ such that $-\frac{p}{2} < iq-jp < 0$. Note that $0 < j < \frac{q}{2}$ since $0 < i < \frac{p}{2}$. In other words, $(\frac{q}{p}) = (-1)^s$, where $s$ is the number of lattice points $(x, y)$, that is, pairs of integers $x$, $y$ satisfying \begin{equation} 0 < py - qx < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < x < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < y < \frac{q}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: (q/p) = (-1)^s, s lattice points in a strip

nodes.name: (p/q) = (-1)^t similarly
nodes.statement: Similarly, $(\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^t$ where $t$ is the number of lattice points $(x, y)$ with \begin{equation} 0 < qx - py < \frac{q}{2}, \quad 0 < x < \frac{p}{2}, \quad 0 < y < \frac{q}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: (p/q) = (-1)^t similarly

nodes.name: Rectangle and lines parallel to the diagonal
nodes.statement: Now look at the rectangle with side lengths $\frac{p}{2}$, $\frac{q}{2}$, and draw the two lines parallel to the diagonal $py = qx$, $y = \frac{q}{p}x + \frac{1}{2}$ or $py - qx = \frac{p}{2}$, respectively, $y = \frac{q}{p} \left(x - \frac{1}{2}\right)$ or $qx - py = \frac{q}{2}$. The proof is now quickly completed by the following three observations:
nodes.statement_short: Rectangle and lines parallel to the diagonal

nodes.name: 1. No lattice points on the lines
nodes.statement: There are no lattice points on the diagonal and the two parallels. This is so because $py = qx$ would imply $p \mid x$, which cannot be. For the parallels observe that $py - qx$ is an integer while $\frac{p}{2}$ and $\frac{q}{2}$ are not.
nodes.statement_short: 1. No lattice points on the lines

nodes.name: 2. The strips contain s + t points
nodes.statement: The lattice points observing \eqref{eq:s} are precisely the points in the upper strip $0 < py - qx < \frac{p}{2}$, and those of \eqref{eq:t} the points in the lower strip $0 < qx - py < \frac{q}{2}$. Hence the number of lattice points in the two strips is $s + t$.
nodes.statement_short: 2. The strips contain s + t points

nodes.name: 3. Outer regions have equally many points
nodes.statement: The outer regions $R : py - qx > \frac{p}{2}$ and $S: qx - py > \frac{q}{2}$ contain the \textit{same} number of points. To see this consider the map $\varphi: R \to S$ which maps $(x, y)$ to $\left(\frac{p+1}{2} - x, \frac{q+1}{2} - y\right)$ and check that $\varphi$ is an involution.
nodes.statement_short: 3. Outer regions have equally many points

nodes.name: Parity gives the reciprocity law
nodes.statement: Since the total number of lattice points in the rectangle is $\frac{p-1}{2} \cdot \frac{q-1}{2}$, we infer that $s + t$ and $\frac{p-1}{2} \cdot \frac{q-1}{2}$ have the same parity, and so \[ (\frac{q}{p}) (\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^{s+t} = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \qedhere \]
nodes.statement_short: Parity gives the reciprocity law

nodes.name: Seek an element of order n = |F^*|
nodes.statement: Let $F^*$ be the multiplicative group of the field $F$, with $|F^*| = n$. Writing $\ord(a)$ for the order of an element, that is, the smallest positive integer $k$ such that $a^k = 1$, we want to find an element $a \in F^*$ with $\ord(a) = n$.
nodes.statement_short: Seek an element of order n = |F^*|

nodes.name: Classify by order: n = sum psi(d)
nodes.statement: If $\ord(b) = d$, then by Lagrange's theorem, $d$ divides $n$. Classifying the elements according to their order, we have \begin{equation} n = \sum_{d \mid n} \psi(d), \quad \text{where } \psi(d) = \#\{b\in F^*: \ord(b) = d\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Classify by order: n = sum psi(d)

nodes.name: Elements of order d are powers b^i
nodes.statement: If $\ord(b) = d$, then every element $b^i$ ($i = 1, \dots, d$) satisfies $(b^i)^d = 1$ and is therefore a root of the polynomial $x^d - 1$. But, since $F$ is a field, $x^d - 1$ has at most $d$ roots, and so the elements $b, b^2, \dots, b^d = 1$ are precisely these roots. In particular, every element of order $d$ is of the form $b^i$.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of order d are powers b^i

nodes.name: psi(d) <= phi(d)
nodes.statement: On the other hand, it is easily checked that $\ord(b^i) = \frac{d}{(i, d)}$, where $(i, d)$ denotes the greatest common divisor of $i$ and $d$. Hence $\ord(b^i) = d$ if and only if $(i, d) = 1$, that is, if $i$ and $d$ are relatively prime. Denoting \textit{Euler's function} by $\varphi(d) = \#\{i : 1 \le i \le d, (i, d) = 1\}$, we thus have $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$ whenever $\psi(d) > 0$. Looking at \eqref{eq:sum_psi} we find \[ n = \sum_{d \mid n} \psi(d) \le \sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d). \]
nodes.statement_short: psi(d) <= phi(d)

nodes.name: sum phi(d) = n forces psi(n) >= 1
nodes.statement: But as we are going to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{d \mid n} \varphi(d) = n, \end{equation} we must have $\psi(d) = \varphi(d)$ for all $d$. In particular, $\psi(n) = \varphi(n) \ge 1$, and so there is an element of order $n$.
nodes.statement_short: sum phi(d) = n forces psi(n) >= 1

nodes.name: Prove sum phi(d) = n via reduced fractions k/n
nodes.statement: The following (folklore) proof of \eqref{eq:sum_phi} belongs in the Book as well. Consider the $n$ fractions \[ \frac{1}{n}, \frac{2}{n}, \dots, \frac{k}{n}, \dots, \frac{n}{n}, \] reduce them to the lowest term $\frac{k}{n} = \frac{i}{d}$ with $1 \le i \le d$, $(i, d) = 1$, $d \mid n$, and check that the denominator $d$ appears precisely $\varphi(d)$ times.
nodes.statement_short: Prove sum phi(d) = n via reduced fractions k/n

nodes.name: F^* is cyclic
nodes.statement: The multiplicative group $F^* = F \setminus \{0\}$ is cyclic of size $q^{p-1} - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: F^* is cyclic

nodes.name: Fermat gives an element zeta of order p
nodes.statement: Since by Fermat's little theorem $p$ is a divisor of $q^{p-1} - 1$, there exists an element $\zeta \in F$ of order $p$, that is, $\zeta^p = 1$, and $\zeta$ generates the subgroup $\{\zeta, \zeta^2, \dots, \zeta^p = 1\}$ of $F^*$.
nodes.statement_short: Fermat gives an element zeta of order p

nodes.name: Powers of zeta give the decomposition of x^p - 1
nodes.statement: Note that any $\zeta^i$ ($i \ne p$) is again a generator. Hence we obtain the polynomial decomposition $x^p - 1 = (x - \zeta) (x - \zeta^2) \cdots (x - \zeta^p)$.
nodes.statement_short: Powers of zeta give the decomposition of x^p - 1

nodes.name: Introduce the Gauss sum G
nodes.statement: The second proof does not use Gauss' lemma, instead it employs so-called ``Gauss sums'' in finite fields. Gauss invented them in his study of the equation $x^p - 1 = 0$ and the arithmetical properties of the field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ (called cyclotomic field), where $\zeta$ is a $p$-th root of unity. They have been the starting point for the search for higher reciprocity laws in general number fields. Consider the \textit{Gauss sum} \[ G := \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{i}{p}) \zeta^i \in F, \] where $(\frac{i}{p})$ is the Legendre symbol. For the proof we derive two different expressions for $G^q$ and then set them equal.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Gauss sum G

nodes.name: Context: Gauss sums
nodes.statement: The second proof does not use Gauss' lemma, instead it employs so-called ``Gauss sums'' in finite fields. Gauss invented them in his study of the equation $x^p - 1 = 0$ and the arithmetical properties of the field $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta)$ (called cyclotomic field), where $\zeta$ is a $p$-th root of unity. They have been the starting point for the search for higher reciprocity laws in general number fields.
nodes.statement_short: Context: Gauss sums

nodes.name: Define G; plan to compute G^q twice
nodes.statement: Consider the \textit{Gauss sum} \[ G := \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{i}{p}) \zeta^i \in F, \] where $(\frac{i}{p})$ is the Legendre symbol. For the proof we derive two different expressions for $G^q$ and then set them equal.
nodes.statement_short: Define G; plan to compute G^q twice

nodes.name: G^q = (q/p) G
nodes.statement: \textbf{First expression.} We have \begin{equation} G^q = \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{i}{p})^q \zeta^{iq} = \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{i}{p}) \zeta^{iq} = (\frac{q}{p}) \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{iq}{p}) \zeta^{iq} = (\frac{q}{p}) G, \end{equation} where the first equality follows from $(a + b)^q = a^q + b^q$, the second uses that $(\frac{i}{p})^q = (\frac{i}{p})$ since $q$ is odd, the third one is derived from \eqref{eq:product_rule}, which yields $(\frac{i}{p}) = (\frac{q}{p}) (\frac{iq}{p})$, and the last one holds since $iq$ runs with $i$ through all nonzero residues modulo $p$.
nodes.statement_short: G^q = (q/p) G

nodes.name: Assuming G^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p, derive reciprocity
nodes.statement: \textbf{Second expression.} Suppose we can prove \begin{equation} G^2 = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}} p, \end{equation} then we are quickly done. Indeed, \begin{equation} G^q = G (G^2)^{\frac{q-1}{2}} = G (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}} p^{\frac{q-1}{2}} = G (\frac{p}{q}) (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \end{equation} Equating the expressions in \eqref{eq:first-expression} and \eqref{eq:second-expression} and cancelling $G$, which is nonzero by \eqref{eq:G^2}, we find $(\frac{q}{p}) = (\frac{p}{q}) (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}$, and thus \[ (\frac{q}{p}) (\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assuming G^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p, derive reciprocity

nodes.name: Reduce to G^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p
nodes.statement: \textbf{Second expression.} Suppose we can prove \begin{equation} G^2 = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}} p, \end{equation} then we are quickly done.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to G^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p

nodes.name: G^q = (p/q)(-1)^{...} G
nodes.statement: Indeed, \begin{equation} G^q = G (G^2)^{\frac{q-1}{2}} = G (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}} p^{\frac{q-1}{2}} = G (\frac{p}{q}) (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Equate and cancel G
nodes.statement: Equating the expressions in \eqref{eq:first-expression} and \eqref{eq:second-expression} and cancelling $G$, which is nonzero by \eqref{eq:G^2}, we find $(\frac{q}{p}) = (\frac{p}{q}) (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}$, and thus \[ (\frac{q}{p}) (\frac{p}{q}) = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2} \frac{q-1}{2}}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equate and cancel G

nodes.name: Verify G^2 = (-1)^{(p-1)/2} p
nodes.statement: It remains to verify \eqref{eq:G^2}, and for this we first make two simple observations: \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{i=1}^{p} \zeta^i = 0$ and thus $\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} \zeta^i = -1$. Just note that $-\sum_{i=1}^{p} \zeta^i$ is the coefficient of $x^{p-1}$ in $x^p - 1 = \prod_{i=1}^{p} (x - \zeta^i)$, and thus 0. \item $\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} (\frac{k}{p}) = 0$ and thus $\sum_{k=1}^{p-2} (\frac{k}{p}) = - (\frac{-1}{p})$, since there are equally many quadratic residues and nonresidues. \end{itemize} We have \[ G^2 = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} (\frac{i}{p}) \zeta^i\right) \left(\sum_{j=1}^{p-1} (\frac{j}{p}) \zeta^j\right) = \sum_{i,j} (\frac{ij}{p}) \zeta^{i+j}. \] Setting $j \equiv ik \pmod{p}$ we find \[ G^2 = \sum_{i,k} (\frac{k}{p}) \zeta^{i(1+k)} = \sum_{k=1}^{p-1} (\frac{k}{p}) \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} \zeta^{(1+k)i}. \] For $k = p - 1 \equiv -1 \pmod{p}$ this gives $(\frac{-1}{p}) (p - 1)$, since $\zeta^{1+k} = 1$. Move $k = p - 1$ in front and write \[ G^2 = (\frac{-1}{p}) (p - 1) + \sum_{k=1}^{p-2} (\frac{k}{p}) \sum_{i=1}^{p-1} \zeta^{(1+k)i}. \] Since $\zeta^{1+k}$ is a generator of the group for $k \ne p - 1$, the inner sum equals $\sum_{i=1}^{p-1} \zeta^i = -1$ for all $k \ne p - 1$ by our first observation. Hence the second summand is $-\sum_{k=1}^{p-2} (\frac{k}{p}) = (\frac{-1}{p})$ by our second observation. It follows that $G^2 = (\frac{-1}{p}) p$ and thus with Euler's criterion $G^2 = (-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}} p$, which completes the proof.

nodes.name: Two simple observations
