nodes.statement: There is another nice proof, due to Michael D.\ Hirschhorn. It uses Bernoulli's inequality, which says \[ (1+t)^{n+1} \ge 1 + (n+1)t \qquad \text{for real } t \ge -1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use Bernoulli's inequality

nodes.name: Set t as the ratio of means minus 1
nodes.statement: Suppose $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n+1} > 0$ and set \[ t = \frac{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_{n+1}}{n+1}}{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n}} - 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Set t as the ratio of means minus 1

nodes.name: Bernoulli gives the inductive step
nodes.statement: By Bernoulli, \[ \left(\frac{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_{n+1}}{n+1}}{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n}}\right)^{n+1} \ge 1 + (n+1)\left(\frac{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_{n+1}}{n+1}}{\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n}} - 1\right) = \frac{n\, a_{n+1}}{a_1 + \cdots + a_n}, \] which translates into \[ \left(\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_{n+1}}{n+1}\right)^{n+1} \ge a_{n+1} \left(\frac{a_1 + \cdots + a_n}{n}\right)^n, \] and the arithmetic-geometric mean inequality follows by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Bernoulli gives the inductive step

nodes.name: Coefficients give sum y_i^2 in terms of a_{n-1}, a_{n-2}, y
nodes.statement: Let $y$ be one of the roots and $y_1, \dots, y_{n-1}$ the others. Then the polynomial is $(x-y)(x-y_1)\cdots(x-y_{n-1})$. Thus by comparing coefficients \begin{align*} -a_{n-1} &= y + y_1 + \cdots + y_{n-1}, \\ a_{n-2} &= y(y_1 + \cdots + y_{n-1}) + \sum_{i<j} y_i y_j, \end{align*} and so $a_{n-1}^2 - 2a_{n-2} - y^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{n-1} y_i^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients give sum y_i^2 in terms of a_{n-1}, a_{n-2}, y

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz gives a quadratic inequality in y
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy–Schwarz gives a quadratic inequality in y

nodes.name: y lies between the roots of the quadratic
nodes.statement: Thus $y$ (and hence all $y_i$) lie between the two roots of the quadratic function, and these roots are our bounds.
nodes.statement_short: y lies between the roots of the quadratic

nodes.name: Proof of (2/3)T <= A
nodes.statement: \textbf{Proof of $\frac{2}{3}T \le A$.} Since $f(x)$ has only real roots, and none of them in the open interval $(-1,1)$, it can be written (apart from a constant positive factor which cancels out) in the form \[ f(x) = (1-x^2)\prod_i (\alpha_i - x)\prod_j (\beta_j + x) \] with $\alpha_i \ge 1$, $\beta_j \ge 1$. Hence $A = \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx$. By making the substitution $x \to -x$, we find that also $A = \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\prod_i(\alpha_i + x)\prod_j(\beta_j - x)\,dx$, and hence by the inequality of the arithmetic and the geometric mean (note that all factors are $\ge 0$): \begin{align*} A &= \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-x^2)\prod(\alpha_i - x)\prod(\beta_j + x) + (1-x^2)\prod(\alpha_i + x)\prod(\beta_j - x)\right] dx \\ &\ge \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - x^2)\prod(\beta_j^2 - x^2)\right]^{1/2} dx \\ &\ge \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - 1)\prod(\beta_j^2 - 1)\right]^{1/2} dx \\ &= \frac{4}{3}\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - 1)\prod(\beta_j^2 - 1)\right]^{1/2}. \end{align*} Computing $f'(1)$ and $f'(-1)$ from the product form, we find $f'(1) = -2\prod(\alpha_i - 1)\prod(\beta_j + 1)$ and $f'(-1) = 2\prod(\alpha_i + 1)\prod(\beta_j - 1)$, hence $-f'(1)f'(-1) = 4\prod(\alpha_i^2-1)\prod(\beta_j^2-1)$, so \[ A \ge \frac{2}{3}(-f'(1)f'(-1))^{1/2}. \] Applying the inequality of the harmonic and geometric mean to $-f'(1)$ and $f'(-1)$, we arrive by formula~(2) for $T$ at \[ A \ge \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{\frac{1}{-f'(1)} + \frac{1}{f'(-1)}} = \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{f'(1)f'(-1)}{f'(1)-f'(-1)} = \frac{2}{3}T. \]
nodes.statement_short: Proof of (2/3)T <= A

nodes.name: Product form of f
nodes.statement: \textbf{Proof of $\frac{2}{3}T \le A$.} Since $f(x)$ has only real roots, and none of them in the open interval $(-1,1)$, it can be written (apart from a constant positive factor which cancels out) in the form \[ f(x) = (1-x^2)\prod_i (\alpha_i - x)\prod_j (\beta_j + x) \] with $\alpha_i \ge 1$, $\beta_j \ge 1$. Hence $A = \int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx$.
nodes.statement_short: Product form of f

nodes.name: Symmetrize and apply AM-GM
nodes.statement: By making the substitution $x \to -x$, we find that also $A = \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\prod_i(\alpha_i + x)\prod_j(\beta_j - x)\,dx$, and hence by the inequality of the arithmetic and the geometric mean (note that all factors are $\ge 0$): \begin{align*} A &= \int_{-1}^{1} \frac{1}{2}\left[(1-x^2)\prod(\alpha_i - x)\prod(\beta_j + x) + (1-x^2)\prod(\alpha_i + x)\prod(\beta_j - x)\right] dx \\ &\ge \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - x^2)\prod(\beta_j^2 - x^2)\right]^{1/2} dx \\ &\ge \int_{-1}^{1} (1-x^2)\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - 1)\prod(\beta_j^2 - 1)\right]^{1/2} dx \\ &= \frac{4}{3}\left[\prod(\alpha_i^2 - 1)\prod(\beta_j^2 - 1)\right]^{1/2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetrize and apply AM-GM

nodes.name: A >= (2/3) sqrt(-f'(1) f'(-1))
nodes.statement: Computing $f'(1)$ and $f'(-1)$ from the product form, we find $f'(1) = -2\prod(\alpha_i - 1)\prod(\beta_j + 1)$ and $f'(-1) = 2\prod(\alpha_i + 1)\prod(\beta_j - 1)$, hence $-f'(1)f'(-1) = 4\prod(\alpha_i^2-1)\prod(\beta_j^2-1)$, so \[ A \ge \frac{2}{3}(-f'(1)f'(-1))^{1/2}. \]

nodes.name: HM-GM gives A >= (2/3)T
nodes.statement: Applying the inequality of the harmonic and geometric mean to $-f'(1)$ and $f'(-1)$, we arrive by formula~(2) for $T$ at \[ A \ge \frac{2}{3}\cdot\frac{2}{\frac{1}{-f'(1)} + \frac{1}{f'(-1)}} = \frac{4}{3}\cdot\frac{f'(1)f'(-1)}{f'(1)-f'(-1)} = \frac{2}{3}T. \]
nodes.statement_short: HM-GM gives A >= (2/3)T

nodes.name: Upper inequality not proved
nodes.statement: \textbf{The inequality $A \le \frac{2}{3}R$:} The book notes ``The reader is invited to search for an equally inspired proof of the second inequality in Theorem~2.'' This half is not formalized in Lean.
nodes.statement_short: Upper inequality not proved

nodes.name: Setup: degrees and handshaking
nodes.statement: This proof, using Cauchy's inequality, is due to Mantel. Let $V = \{1, \dots, n\}$ be the vertex set and $E$ the edge set of $G$. By $d_i$ we denote the degree of $i$, hence $\sum_{i \in V} d_i = 2|E|$ (see chapter \ref{chapter28}).
nodes.statement_short: Setup: degrees and handshaking

nodes.name: d_i + d_j <= n for each edge
nodes.statement: Suppose $ij$ is an edge. Since $G$ has no triangles, we find $d_i + d_j \leq n$ since no vertex is a neighbor of both $i$ and $j$.
nodes.statement_short: d_i + d_j <= n for each edge

nodes.name: Sum over edges and apply Cauchy–Schwarz
nodes.statement: It follows that \[ \sum_{ij \in E} (d_i + d_j) \leq n|E|. \] Note that $d_i$ appears exactly $d_i$ times in the sum, so we get \[ n|E| \geq \sum_{ij \in E} (d_i + d_j) = \sum_{i \in V} d_i^2, \] and hence with Cauchy's inequality applied to the vectors $(d_1, \dots, d_n)$ and $(1, \dots, 1)$, \[ n|E| \geq \sum_{i \in V} d_i^2 \geq \frac{\left( \sum d_i \right)^2}{n} = \frac{4|E|^2}{n}, \] and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Sum over edges and apply Cauchy–Schwarz

nodes.name: Equality case K_{n/2,n/2}
nodes.statement: In the case of equality we find $d_i = d_j$ for all $i, j$, and further $d_i = \frac{n}{2}$ (since $d_i + d_j = n$). Since $G$ is triangle-free, $G = K_{n/2, n/2}$ is immediately seen from this.
nodes.statement_short: Equality case K_{n/2,n/2}

nodes.name: Largest independent set A of size α
nodes.statement: The following proof of Theorem~3, using the inequality of the arithmetic and the geometric mean, is a folklore Book Proof. Let $\alpha$ be the size of a largest independent set $A$, and set $\beta = n - \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Largest independent set A of size α

nodes.name: d_i <= α
nodes.statement: Since $G$ is triangle-free, the neighbors of a vertex $i$ form an independent set, and we infer $d_i \le \alpha$ for all $i$.
nodes.statement_short: d_i <= α

nodes.name: |E| <= αβ <= n^2/4
nodes.statement: The set $B = V \setminus A$ of size $\beta$ meets every edge of $G$. Counting the edges of $G$ according to their endvertices in $B$, we obtain $|E| \le \sum_{i \in B} d_i$. The inequality of the arithmetic and geometric mean now yields \[ |E| \le \sum_{i \in B} d_i \le \alpha\beta \le \left(\frac{\alpha + \beta}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{n^2}{4}, \] and again the case of equality is easily dealt with.

nodes.name: |p(z)| > |p(0)| on a large circle
nodes.statement: The rest is easy. Clearly, $p(z)z^{-n}$ approaches the leading coefficient $c_n$ of $p(z)$ as $|z|$ goes to infinity. Hence $|p(z)|$ goes to infinity as well with $|z| \to \infty$. Consequently, there exists $R_1 > 0$ such that $|p(z)| > |p(0)|$ for all points $z$ on the circle $\{ z : |z| = R_1 \}$.
nodes.statement_short: |p(z)| > |p(0)| on a large circle

nodes.name: Minimum attained in the interior
nodes.statement: Furthermore, our third fact (C) tells us that in the compact set $D_1 = \{ z : |z| \leq R_1 \}$ the continuous real-valued function $|p(z)|$ attains the minimum value at some point $z_0$. Because of $|p(z)| > |p(0)|$ for $z$ on the boundary of $D_1$, $z_0$ must lie in the interior.
nodes.statement_short: Minimum attained in the interior

nodes.name: The minimum is 0
nodes.statement: But by d'Alembert's lemma \ref{argand_inequality} this minimum value $|p(z_0)|$ must be $0$ — and this is the whole proof.
nodes.statement_short: The minimum is 0

nodes.name: Multiple roots of p are roots of p'
nodes.statement: Let $b_1 < \cdots < b_r$ be the roots of $p(x)$ with multiplicities $s_1, \ldots, s_r$, $\sum_{j=1}^{r} s_j = n$. From $p(x) = (x - b_j)^{s_j} h(x)$ we infer that $b_j$ is a root of $p'(x)$ if $s_j \geq 2$, and the multiplicity of $b_j$ in $p'(x)$ is $s_j - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiple roots of p are roots of p'

nodes.name: Rolle roots are simple by degree count
nodes.statement: Furthermore, there is a root of $p'(x)$ between $b_1$ and $b_2$, another root between $b_2$ and $b_3, \ldots$, and one between $b_{r-1}$ and $b_r$, and all these roots must be single roots, since $\sum_{j=1}^{r} (s_j - 1) + (r - 1)$ counts already up to the degree $n - 1$ of $p'(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rolle roots are simple by degree count

nodes.name: Multiple roots of p' are roots of p
nodes.statement: Consequently, the multiple roots of $p'(x)$ can only occur among the roots of $p(x)$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiple roots of p' are roots of p

nodes.name: Roots: nothing to show
nodes.statement: If $x = a_i$ is a root of $p(x)$, then there is nothing to show.
nodes.statement_short: Roots: nothing to show

nodes.name: Logarithmic derivative
nodes.statement: Assume then $x$ is not a root. The product rule of differentiation yields \[ p'(x) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{p(x)}{x - a_k}, \quad \text{that is,} \quad \frac{p'(x)}{p(x)} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{x - a_k}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Logarithmic derivative

nodes.name: Second derivative is negative
nodes.statement: Differentiating this again we have \[ \frac{p''(x)p(x) - p'(x)^2}{p(x)^2} = - \sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{(x - a_k)^2} < 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Second derivative is negative

nodes.name: Odd parts of the numbers
nodes.statement: Write every number $a \in A$ in the form $a = 2^k m$, where $m$ is an odd number between $1$ and $2n - 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Odd parts of the numbers

nodes.name: Pigeonhole: two share an odd part
nodes.statement: Since there are $n + 1$ numbers in $A$, but only $n$ different odd parts, there must be two numbers in $A$ with the same odd part. Hence one is a multiple of the other.
nodes.statement_short: Pigeonhole: two share an odd part

nodes.name: Define t_i
nodes.statement: This time the application of the pigeon-hole principle is not immediate. Associate to each $a_i$ the number $t_i$, which is the length of a longest increasing subsequence starting at $a_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Define t_i

nodes.name: Case t_i >= m+1
nodes.statement: If $t_i \geq m+1$ for some $i$, then we have an increasing subsequence of length $m+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Case t_i >= m+1

nodes.name: Case all t_i <= m: n+1 equal labels
nodes.statement: Suppose then that $t_i \leq m$ for all $i$. The function $f : a_i \mapsto t_i$ mapping $\{a_1, \dots, a_{mn+1}\}$ to $\{1, \dots, m\}$ tells us by~(1) that there is some $s \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ such that $f(a_i) = s$ for $\frac{mn}{m} + 1 = n + 1$ numbers $a_i$. Let $a_{j_1}, a_{j_2}, \dots, a_{j_{n+1}}$ $(j_1 < \cdots < j_{n+1})$ be these numbers.
nodes.statement_short: Case all t_i <= m: n+1 equal labels

nodes.name: Equal labels form a decreasing subsequence
nodes.statement: Now look at two consecutive numbers $a_{j_i}, a_{j_{i+1}}$. If $a_{j_i} < a_{j_{i+1}}$, then we would obtain an increasing subsequence of length $s$ starting at $a_{j_{i+1}}$, and consequently an increasing subsequence of length $s+1$ starting at $a_{j_i}$, which cannot be since $f(a_{j_i}) = s$. We thus obtain a decreasing subsequence $a_{j_1} > a_{j_2} > \cdots > a_{j_{n+1}}$ of length $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Equal labels form a decreasing subsequence

nodes.name: Prefix sums modulo n
nodes.statement: For the proof we set $N = \{0, 1, \dots, n\}$ and $R = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$. Consider the map $f : N \to R$, where $f(m)$ is the remainder of $a_1 + \cdots + a_m$ upon division by $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Prefix sums modulo n

nodes.name: Two prefix sums agree mod n
nodes.statement: Since $|N| = n+1 > n = |R|$, it follows that there are two sums $a_1 + \cdots + a_k, a_1 + \cdots + a_{\ell}$ $(k < \ell)$ with the same remainder, where the first sum may be the empty sum denoted by $0$. It follows that \[ \sum_{i=k+1}^{\ell} a_i = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} a_i - \sum_{i=1}^{k} a_i \] has remainder $0$ --- end of proof.
nodes.statement_short: Two prefix sums agree mod n

nodes.name: Column count gives sum t(j)
nodes.statement: Consider the matrix $A$ (as above) for the integers $1$ up to $n$. Counting by columns we get $\sum_{j=1}^{n} t(j)$.
nodes.statement_short: Column count gives sum t(j)

nodes.name: Row count gives sum floor(n/i) <= n H_n
nodes.statement: How many $1$'s are in row $i$? Easy enough, the $1$'s correspond to the multiples of $i$: $1 \cdot i, 2 \cdot i, \dots$, and the last multiple not exceeding $n$ is $\lfloor n/i \rfloor \cdot i$. Hence we obtain \[ \bar{t}(n) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} t(j) = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{i} \right\rfloor \leq \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{n}{i} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{1}{i} = H_n, \] where the error in each summand, when passing from $\lfloor n/i \rfloor$ to $n/i$, is less than $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Row count gives sum floor(n/i) <= n H_n

nodes.name: Combine with log n < H_n < log n + 1
nodes.statement: Together with the standard estimates $\log n < H_n < \log n + 1$ this gives $\log n - 1 < \bar{t}(n) \leq H_n < \log n + 1$. Thus we have proved the remarkable result that, while $t(n)$ is totally erratic, the average $\bar{t}(n)$ behaves beautifully: It differs from $\log n$ by less than $1$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with log n < H_n < log n + 1

nodes.name: Count cherries S in a C4-free graph
nodes.statement: Let us tackle the general problem. Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices without a $4$-cycle. We count the following set $S$ in two ways: $S$ is the set of pairs $(u, \{v, w\})$ where $u$ is adjacent to $v$ and to $w$, with $v \neq w$. In other words, we count all occurrences of a ``cherry'' (path of length~$2$ centered at~$u$).
nodes.statement_short: Count cherries S in a C4-free graph

nodes.name: Sum of binom(d(u),2) <= binom(n,2)
nodes.statement: Summing over $u$, we find $|S| = \sum_{u \in V} \binom{d(u)}{2}$. On the other hand, every pair $\{v, w\}$ has at most one common neighbor (by the $C_4$-condition). Hence $|S| \leq \binom{n}{2}$, and we conclude \[ \sum_{u \in V} \binom{d(u)}{2} \leq \binom{n}{2} \] or \[ \sum_{u \in V} d(u)^2 \leq n(n-1) + \sum_{u \in V} d(u). \tag{5} \]
nodes.statement_short: Sum of binom(d(u),2) <= binom(n,2)

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz on the degree vector
nodes.statement: Next we apply the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality to the vectors $(d(u_1), \dots, d(u_n))$ and $(1, 1, \dots, 1)$, obtaining \[ \left(\sum_{u \in V} d(u)\right)^2 \leq n \sum_{u \in V} d(u)^2, \] and hence by~(5) \[ \left(\sum_{u \in V} d(u)\right)^2 \leq n^2(n-1) + n \sum_{u \in V} d(u). \]
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy–Schwarz on the degree vector

nodes.name: Handshaking gives a quadratic inequality in |E|
nodes.statement: Invoking~(4) we find \[ 4|E|^2 \leq n^2(n-1) + 2n|E| \] or \[ |E|^2 - \frac{n}{2}|E| - \frac{n^2(n-1)}{4} \leq 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Handshaking gives a quadratic inequality in |E|

nodes.name: Solve the quadratic for |E|
nodes.statement: Solving the corresponding quadratic equation we thus obtain the following result of Istv\'an Reiman.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the quadratic for |E|

nodes.name: Prove the number of tricolored triangles is odd
nodes.statement: We will prove a stronger statement: The number of tricolored triangles is not only nonzero, it is always \emph{odd}.
nodes.statement_short: Prove the number of tricolored triangles is odd

nodes.name: Partial dual graph through 1-2 edges
nodes.statement: Consider the dual graph to the triangulation, but don't take all its edges --- only those which cross an edge that has endvertices with the (different) colors $1$ and $2$. Thus we get a ``partial dual graph'' which has degree $1$ at all vertices that correspond to tricolored triangles, degree $2$ for all triangles in which the two colors $1$ and $2$ appear, and degree $0$ for triangles that do not have both colors $1$ and $2$. Thus only the tricolored triangles correspond to vertices of odd degree (of degree $1$).
nodes.statement_short: Partial dual graph through 1-2 edges

nodes.name: The outer vertex has odd degree
nodes.statement: However, the vertex of the dual graph which corresponds to the outside of the triangulation has odd degree: in fact, along the big edge from $V_1$ to $V_2$, there is an odd number of changes between $1$ and $2$. Thus an odd number of edges of the partial dual graph crosses this big edge, while the other big edges cannot have both $1$ and $2$ occurring as colors.
nodes.statement_short: The outer vertex has odd degree

nodes.name: Handshaking parity gives an odd count
nodes.statement: Now since the number of odd-degree vertices in any finite graph is even (by equation~(4)), we find that the number of small triangles with three different colors (corresponding to odd inside vertices of our dual graph) is odd.
nodes.statement_short: Handshaking parity gives an odd count

nodes.name: Reduce to the standard triangle Δ
nodes.statement: Let $\Delta$ be the triangle in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with vertices $e_1 = (1,0,0)$, $e_2 = (0,1,0)$, and $e_3 = (0,0,1)$. It suffices to prove that every continuous map $f : \Delta \to \Delta$ has a fixed point, since $\Delta$ is homeomorphic to $B^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the standard triangle Δ

nodes.name: Triangulations with mesh tending to 0
nodes.statement: We use $\delta(T)$ to denote the maximal length of an edge in a triangulation $T$. One can easily construct an infinite sequence of triangulations $T_1, T_2, \dots$ of $\Delta$ such that the sequence of maximal diameters $\delta(T_k)$ converges to $0$ (for example by iterated barycentric subdivision).
nodes.statement_short: Triangulations with mesh tending to 0

nodes.name: Coloring λ(v) by the first negative coordinate
nodes.statement: For each of these triangulations, we define a $3$-coloring of their vertices $v$ by setting $\lambda(v) := \min\{i : f(v)_i < v_i\}$, that is, $\lambda(v)$ is the smallest index $i$ such that the $i$-th coordinate of $f(v) - v$ is negative. If this smallest index $i$ does not exist, then we have found a fixed point and are done: To see this, note that every $v \in \Delta$ lies in the plane $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 1$, hence $\sum_i v_i = 1$. So if $f(v) \neq v$, then at least one of the coordinates of $f(v) - v$ must be negative (and at least one must be positive).
nodes.statement_short: Coloring λ(v) by the first negative coordinate

nodes.name: The coloring satisfies Sperner's assumptions
nodes.statement: Let us check that this coloring satisfies the assumptions of Sperner's lemma. First, the vertex $e_i$ must receive color $i$, since the only possible negative component of $f(e_i) - e_i$ is the $i$-th component. Moreover, if $v$ lies on the edge opposite to $e_i$, then $v_i = 0$, so the $i$-th component of $f(v) - v$ cannot be negative, and hence $v$ does not get the color $i$.
nodes.statement_short: The coloring satisfies Sperner's assumptions

nodes.name: Vertices e_i get color i
nodes.statement: First, the vertex $e_i$ must receive color $i$, since the only possible negative component of $f(e_i) - e_i$ is the $i$-th component.
nodes.statement_short: Vertices e_i get color i

nodes.name: Boundary vertices avoid the opposite color
nodes.statement: Moreover, if $v$ lies on the edge opposite to $e_i$, then $v_i = 0$, so the $i$-th component of $f(v) - v$ cannot be negative, and hence $v$ does not get the color $i$.
nodes.statement_short: Boundary vertices avoid the opposite color

nodes.name: Tricolored triangles converge to a point v
nodes.statement: Sperner's lemma now tells us that in each triangulation $T_k$ there is a tricolored triangle $\{v^{k:1}, v^{k:2}, v^{k:3}\}$ with $\lambda(v^{k:i}) = i$. Since the simplex $\Delta$ is compact, some subsequence of $(v^{k:1})_{k \geq 1}$ has a limit point~$v$. The distances of $v^{k:2}$ and $v^{k:3}$ from $v^{k:1}$ are at most the mesh length $\delta(T_k) \to 0$, so all three sequences converge to the same point~$v$.
nodes.statement_short: Tricolored triangles converge to a point v

nodes.name: No coordinate of f(v) - v is positive, so f(v) = v
nodes.statement: But where is $f(v)$? We know that the first coordinate of $f(v^{k:1})$ is smaller than that of $v^{k:1}$ for all $k$. Now since $f$ is continuous, we derive that the first coordinate of $f(v)$ is smaller or equal to that of $v$. The same reasoning works for the second and third coordinates. Thus none of the coordinates of $f(v) - v$ is positive --- and we have already seen that this contradicts the assumption $f(v) \neq v$.
nodes.statement_short: No coordinate of f(v) - v is positive, so f(v) = v

nodes.name: Maximal chains from permutations
nodes.statement: We follow Lubell's elegant proof via the LYM inequality. Consider all $n!$ permutations $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,n\}$, each generating a maximal chain $\{\sigma(1)\} \subset \{\sigma(1),\sigma(2)\} \subset \cdots \subset \{1,\dots,n\}$.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Maximal chains from permutations

nodes.name: LYM inequality
nodes.statement: A $k$-element set $A$ appears in exactly $k!(n-k)!$ of these chains. Since an antichain $\mathcal{F}$ meets each chain in at most one set, summing over $\mathcal{F}$ gives \[ \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} k_A!(n-k_A)! \le n!, \] i.e.\ $\sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{\binom{n}{|A|}} \le 1$ (the \emph{LYM inequality}).
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: LYM inequality

nodes.name: Bound |F| by the middle binomial coefficient
nodes.statement: Since each summand is at least $1/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, we conclude $|\mathcal{F}| \le \binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Bound |F| by the middle binomial coefficient

nodes.name: Arcs as runs of k consecutive points
nodes.statement: Consider the $n$ points arranged on a circle. Each arc of length $k$ consists of $k$ consecutive points.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Arcs as runs of k consecutive points

nodes.name: At most k pairwise intersecting arcs
nodes.statement: Two arcs of length $k$ on a circle of $n \ge 2k$ points are disjoint if and only if their starting points are at distance $\ge k$. Since there are $n$ possible starting points and each arc ``blocks out'' $2k - 1$ starting points for intersecting arcs, the maximum number of pairwise intersecting arcs is at most $k$. (This lemma is subsumed by the Kruskal--Katona machinery in Mathlib's proof of EKR.)
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: At most k pairwise intersecting arcs

nodes.name: Arrange the ground set on a circle
nodes.statement: We follow Katona's cyclic permutation argument. Arrange $\{1,\dots,n\}$ on a circle.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Arrange the ground set on a circle

nodes.name: At most k arcs per circular permutation
nodes.statement: Among the $n$ arcs of $k$ consecutive elements, at most $k$ can be pairwise intersecting (by the arc lemma). For each of the $(n-1)!$ circular permutations, an intersecting family $\mathcal{F}$ contributes at most $k$ arcs.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: At most k arcs per circular permutation

nodes.name: Double counting gives the bound
nodes.statement: Each $k$-set appears as an arc in exactly $k!(n-k)!$ circular permutations. Double counting gives \[ |\mathcal{F}| \cdot k!(n-k)! \le k \cdot (n-1)!, \] so $|\mathcal{F}| \le \binom{n-1}{k-1}$.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Double counting gives the bound

nodes.name: Necessity; sufficiency by induction
nodes.statement: Necessity is clear: the $m$ distinct representatives of any $m$ sets must lie in their union. For sufficiency, we use induction on $n$.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Necessity; sufficiency by induction

nodes.name: Strict Hall condition: pick any representative
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1:} If Hall's condition holds strictly ($|\bigcup_{i \in S} A_i| \ge |S| + 1$ for every proper nonempty $S \subsetneq \{1,\dots,n\}$), pick any $a_1 \in A_1$ as representative, remove $a_1$ from all sets, and verify that Hall's condition still holds for $A_2 \setminus \{a_1\}, \dots, A_n \setminus \{a_1\}$.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Strict Hall condition: pick any representative

nodes.name: Tight subfamily: apply induction twice
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2:} If some proper nonempty subset $S$ is ``tight'' ($|\bigcup_{i \in S} A_i| = |S|$), first find an SDR for the subfamily $(A_i)_{i \in S}$ by induction. Then show that the remaining sets $(A_j)_{j \notin S}$, with the chosen representatives removed, still satisfy Hall's condition (using tightness of $S$), and apply induction again.
nodes.section: 30 Three famous theorems on finite sets
nodes.statement_short: Tight subfamily: apply induction twice

nodes.name: Notation Q(S) and U(S)
nodes.statement: If $X$ is a random variable with values in $\mathfrak{S}_n$, with probability distribution $\mathbb{Q}$, then we write $\mathbb{Q}(S)$ for the probability that $X$ takes a value in $S \subseteq \mathfrak{S}_n$. Thus $\mathbb{Q}(S) = \text{Prob}[X \in S]$, and in the case of the uniform distribution $\mathbb{Q} = \mathbb{U}$ we get \[ \mathbb{U}(S) = \text{Prob}[X \in S] = \frac{|S|}{n!}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Notation Q(S) and U(S)

nodes.name: Decompose by the stopping time
nodes.statement: For every subset $S \subseteq \mathfrak{S}_n$, we get the probability that after $k$ steps our deck is ordered according to a permutation in $S$ as \[ \mathbb{Q}^*k(S) = \text{Prob}[X_k \in S] = \sum_{j \leq k} \text{Prob}[X_k \in S \land T = j] + \text{Prob}[X_k \in S \land T > k] \] \[ = \sum_{j \leq k} \mathbb{U}(S) \cdot \text{Prob}[T = j] + \text{Prob}[X_k \in S | T > k] \cdot \text{Prob}[T > k] \] \[ = \mathbb{U}(S) (1 - \text{Prob}[T > k]) + \text{Prob}[X_k \in S | T > k] \cdot \text{Prob}[T > k] \] \[ = \mathbb{U}(S) + (\text{Prob}[X_k \in S | T > k] - \mathbb{U}(S)) \cdot \text{Prob}[T > k]. \]
nodes.statement_short: Decompose by the stopping time

nodes.name: Difference of probabilities bounded by Prob[T > k]
nodes.statement: This yields \[ |\mathbb{Q}^*k(S) - \mathbb{U}(S)| \leq \text{Prob}[T > k] \] since \[ \text{Prob}[X_k \in S | T > k] - \mathbb{U}(S) \] is a difference of two probabilities, so it has absolute value at most 1.
nodes.statement_short: Difference of probabilities bounded by Prob[T > k]

nodes.name: Expand p in powers of x_n
nodes.statement: We use induction on $n$, with fact (1) above as the starting case $n = 1$. Let us split $p(x)$ into summands according to the powers of $x_n$, \[ p(x) = g_0 + g_1 x_n + g_2 x_n^2 + \cdots + g_\ell x_n^\ell, \] where $g_i \in F[x_1, \dots, x_{n-1}]$ for $0 \leq i \leq \ell \leq d$, and $g_\ell$ is nonzero. We write every $v \in F^n$ in the form $v = (a, b)$ with $a \in F^{n-1}$, $b \in F$, and estimate the number of roots $p(a, b) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand p in powers of x_n

nodes.name: Roots with g_ℓ(a) = 0
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1.} Roots $(a, b)$ with $g_\ell(a) = 0$. Since $g_\ell \neq 0$ and $\deg g_\ell \leq d - \ell$, by induction the polynomial $g_\ell$ has at most $(d - \ell) q^{n-2}$ roots in $F^{n-1}$, and for each $a$ there are at most $q$ different choices for $b$, which gives at most $(d - \ell)q^{n-1}$ such roots for $p(x)$ in $F^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Roots with g_ℓ(a) = 0

nodes.name: Roots with g_ℓ(a) ≠ 0
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} Roots $(a, b)$ with $g_\ell(a) \neq 0$. Here $p(a, x_n) \in F[x_n]$ is not the zero polynomial in the single variable $x_n$, it has degree $\ell$, and hence for each $a$ by (1) there are at most $\ell$ elements $b$ with $p(a, b) = 0$. Since the number of $a$'s is at most $q^{n-1}$ we get at most $\ell q^{n-1}$ roots for $p(x)$ in this way.
nodes.statement_short: Roots with g_ℓ(a) ≠ 0

nodes.name: Total at most d q^{n-1}
nodes.statement: Summing the two cases gives at most \[ (d - \ell)q^{n-1} + \ell q^{n-1} = dq^{n-1} \] roots for $p(x)$, as asserted.
nodes.statement_short: Total at most d q^{n-1}

nodes.name: Monomial basis of V_d
nodes.statement: Consider the vector space $V_d$ of all polynomials in $F[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ of degree at most $d$. A basis for $V_d$ is provided by the monomials $x_1^{s_1} \dots x_n^{s_n}$ with $\sum s_i \leq d$: \[ 1, x_1, \dots, x_n, x_1^2, x_1 x_2, \dots, x_1^3, \dots, x_n^d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Monomial basis of V_d

nodes.name: Count monomials via increasing sequences
nodes.statement: The following pleasing argument shows that the number of monomials $x_1^{s_1} \dots x_n^{s_n}$ of degree at most $d$ equals the binomial coefficient $\binom{n+d}{d}$. What we want to count is the number of $n$-tuples $(s_1, \dots, s_n)$ of nonnegative integers with $s_1 + \cdots + s_n \leq d$. To do this, we map every $n$-tuple $(s_1, \dots, s_n)$ to the increasing sequence \[ s_1 + 1 < s_1 + s_2 + 2 < \cdots < s_1 + \cdots + s_n + n, \] which determines an $n$-subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, d + n\}$. The map is bijective, so the number of monomials is $\binom{n+d}{d}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count monomials via increasing sequences

nodes.name: Evaluation map has a nonzero kernel
nodes.statement: Next look at the vector space $F^E$ of all functions $f : E \to F$; it has dimension $|E|$, which by assumption is less than $\binom{n+d}{d} = \dim V_d$. The evaluation map $p(x) \mapsto (p(a))_{a \in E}$ from $V_d$ to $F^E$ is a linear map of vector spaces. We conclude that it has a nonzero kernel, containing as desired a nonzero polynomial that vanishes on $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluation map has a nonzero kernel

nodes.name: Assume |K| < binom(q+n-1,n)
nodes.statement: The second inequality is clear from the definition of binomial coefficients. For the first, set again $q = |F|$ and suppose for a contradiction that \[ |K| < \binom{q + n - 1}{n} = \binom{n + q - 1}{q - 1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume |K| < binom(q+n-1,n)

nodes.name: Vanishing polynomial of degree d <= q-1
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{ch35lemma2} there exists a nonzero polynomial $p(x) \in F[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ of degree $d \leq q - 1$ that vanishes on $K$. Let us write \[ p(x) = p_0(x) + p_1(x) + \cdots + p_d(x), \tag{1} \] where $p_i(x)$ is the sum of the monomials of degree $i$; in particular, $p_d(x)$ is nonzero. Since $p(x)$ vanishes on the nonempty set $K$, we have $d > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing polynomial of degree d <= q-1

nodes.name: Line through w in direction v
nodes.statement: Take any $v \in F^n \setminus \{0\}$. By the Kakeya property for this $v$ there exists a $w \in F^n$ such that \[ p(w + tv) = 0 \quad \text{for all} \ t \in F. \]
nodes.statement_short: Line through w in direction v

nodes.name: p_d(v) = 0
nodes.statement: Here comes the trick: Consider $p(w + tv)$ as a polynomial in the single variable $t$. It has degree at most $d \leq q - 1$ but vanishes on all $q$ points of $F$, whence $p(w + tv)$ is the zero polynomial in $t$. Looking at (1) above we see that the coefficient of $t^d$ in $p(w + tv)$ is precisely $p_d(v)$, which must therefore be 0.

nodes.name: p_d vanishes on F^n, contradicting the root bound
nodes.statement: But $v \in F^n \setminus \{0\}$ was arbitrary and $p_d(0) = 0$ since $d > 0$, and we conclude that $p_d(x)$ vanishes on all of $F^n$. Since \[ dq^{n-1} \leq (q - 1)q^{n-1} < q^n, \] Lemma \ref{ch35lemma1}, however, tells us that $p_d(x)$ must then be the zero polynomial — contradiction and end of the proof.
nodes.statement_short: p_d vanishes on F^n, contradicting the root bound

nodes.name: Admissible rows are SDRs
nodes.statement: We apply Hall's theorem \ref{ch30theorem3} (see Chapter \ref{chapter30}). Let $A_j$ be the set of numbers that do not appear in column $j$. An admissible $(r+1)$-st row corresponds then precisely to a system of distinct representatives for the collection $A_1, \dots, A_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Admissible rows are SDRs

nodes.name: Verify Hall's condition by counting
nodes.statement: To prove the lemma we therefore have to verify Hall's condition (H). Every set $A_j$ has size $n - r$, and every element is in precisely $n - r$ sets $A_j$ (since it appears $r$ times in the rectangle). Any $m$ of the sets $A_j$ contain together $m(n - r)$ elements and therefore at least $m$ different ones, which is just condition (H).
nodes.statement_short: Verify Hall's condition by counting

nodes.name: Base case |V| = 1
nodes.statement: We proceed by induction on $|V|$. For $|V| = 1$ there is nothing to prove.
nodes.statement_short: Base case |V| = 1

nodes.name: Kernel K(c) of the vertices allowing color c
nodes.statement: Choose a color $c \in \mathcal{C} = \bigcup_{v \in V} C(v)$ and set \[ A(c) := \{v \in V : c \in C(v)\}. \] By hypothesis, the induced subgraph $G_{A(c)}$ possesses a kernel $K(c)$.
nodes.statement_short: Kernel K(c) of the vertices allowing color c

nodes.name: Color K(c) with c and delete
nodes.statement: Now we color all $v \in K(c)$ with the color $c$ (this is possible since $K(c)$ is independent), and delete $K(c)$ from $G$ and $c$ from $C$. Let $G'$ be the induced subgraph of $G$ on $V \setminus K(c)$ with $C'(v) = C(v) \setminus \{c\}$ as the new list of color sets.
nodes.statement_short: Color K(c) with c and delete

nodes.name: List sizes still exceed out-degrees
nodes.statement: Notice that for each $v \in A(c) \setminus K(c)$, the outdegree $d^+(v)$ is decreased by at least 1 (due to condition (ii) of a kernel). So $d^+(v) + 1 \leq |C'(v)|$ still holds in $\vec{G'}$. The same condition also holds for the vertices outside $A(c)$, since in this case the color sets $C(v)$ remain unchanged.
nodes.statement_short: List sizes still exceed out-degrees

nodes.name: Apply the induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: The new graph $G'$ contains fewer vertices than $G$, and we are done by induction.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the induction hypothesis

nodes.name: First stage of proposals
nodes.statement: Consider the following algorithm. In the first stage all men $u \in X$ propose to their top choice. If a girl receives more than one proposal she picks the one she likes best and keeps him on a string, and if she receives just one proposal she keeps that one on a string. The remaining men are rejected and form the reservoir $R$.
nodes.statement_short: First stage of proposals

nodes.name: Iterate proposals
nodes.statement: In the second stage all men in $R$ propose to their next choice. The women compare the proposals (together with the one on the string, if there is one), pick their favorite and put him on the string. The rest is rejected and forms the new set $R$. Now the men in $R$ propose to their next choice, and so on.
nodes.statement_short: Iterate proposals

nodes.name: Drop-outs and termination
nodes.statement: A man who has proposed to his last choice and is again rejected drops out from further consideration (as well as from the reservoir). Clearly, after some time the reservoir $R$ is empty, and at this point the algorithm stops.
nodes.statement_short: Drop-outs and termination

nodes.name: Girls' partners improve monotonically
nodes.statement: Notice first that the men on the string of a particular girl move there in increasing preference (of the girl) since at each stage the girl compares the new proposals with the present mate and then picks the new favorite.
nodes.statement_short: Girls' partners improve monotonically

nodes.name: Every non-matching edge is blocked
nodes.statement: Hence if $uv \in E$ but $uv \notin M$, then either $u$ never proposed to $v$ in which case he found a better mate before he even got around to $v$, implying $uy \in M$ with $y > v$ in $N(u)$, or $u$ proposed to $v$ but was rejected, implying $xv \in M$ with $x > u$ in $N(v)$. But this is exactly the condition of a stable matching.
nodes.statement_short: Every non-matching edge is blocked

nodes.name: Orient S_n via a Latin square
nodes.statement: As before we denote the vertices of $S_n$ by $(i, j)$, $1 \leq i, j \leq n$. Thus $(i, j)$ and $(r, s)$ are adjacent if and only if $i = r$ or $j = s$. Take any Latin square $L$ with letters from $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ and denote by $L(i, j)$ the entry in cell $(i, j)$. Next make $S_n$ into a directed graph $\vec{S}_n$ by orienting the horizontal edges $(i, j) \rightarrow (i, j')$ if $L(i, j) < L(i, j')$ and the vertical edges $(i, j) \rightarrow (i', j)$ if $L(i, j) > L(i', j)$. Thus, horizontally we orient from the smaller to the larger element, and vertically the other way around. (In the margin we have an example for $n = 3$.)
nodes.statement_short: Orient S_n via a Latin square

nodes.name: All out-degrees equal n - 1
nodes.statement: Notice that we obtain $d^+(i, j) = n - 1$ for all $(i, j)$. In fact, if $L(i, j) = k$, then $n - k$ cells in row $i$ contain an entry larger than $k$, and $k - 1$ cells in column $j$ have an entry smaller than $k$.
nodes.statement_short: All out-degrees equal n - 1

nodes.name: Reduce to kernels; bipartite graph of a subset A
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{ch38lemma1} it remains to show that every induced subgraph of $\vec{S}_n$ possesses a kernel. Consider a subset $A \subseteq V$, and let $X$ be the set of rows of $L$, and $Y$ the set of its columns. Associate to $A$ the bipartite graph $G = (X \cup Y, A)$, where every $(i, j) \in A$ is represented by the edge $ij$ with $i \in X, j \in Y$. In the example in the margin the cells of $A$ are shaded.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to kernels; bipartite graph of a subset A

nodes.name: Stable matching M of G
nodes.statement: The orientation on $S_n$ naturally induces a ranking on the neighborhoods in $G = (X \cup Y, A)$ by setting $j' > j$ in $N(i)$ if $(i, j) \rightarrow (i, j')$ in $\vec{S}_n$ respectively $i' > i$ in $N(j)$ if $(i, j) \rightarrow (i', j)$. By Lemma \ref{ch38lemma2}, $G = (X \cup Y, A)$ possesses a stable matching $M$. This $M$, viewed as a subset of $A$, is our desired kernel!
nodes.statement_short: Stable matching M of G

nodes.name: M is a kernel
nodes.statement: To see why, note first that $M$ is independent in $A$ since for edges in $G = (X \cup Y, A)$ they do not share an endvertex $i$ or $j$. Secondly, if $(i, j) \in A \setminus M$, then by the definition of a stable matching there either exists $(i, j') \in M$ with $j' > j$ or $(i', j) \in M$ with $i' > i$, which for $\vec{S}_n$ means $(i, j) \rightarrow (i, j') \in M$ or $(i, j) \rightarrow (i', j) \in M$, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: M is a kernel

nodes.name: Triangulate the polygon
nodes.statement: First of all, let us draw $n - 3$ noncrossing diagonals between corners of the walls until the interior is triangulated. For example, we can draw 9 diagonals in the museum depicted in the margin to produce a triangulation. It does not matter which triangulation we choose, any one will do. Now think of the new figure as a plane graph with the corners as vertices and the walls and diagonals as edges.
nodes.statement_short: Triangulate the polygon

nodes.name: Claim: the triangulation graph is 3-colorable
nodes.statement: \textbf{Claim.} \textit{This graph is 3-colorable.} For $n = 3$ there is nothing to prove. Now for $n > 3$ pick any two vertices $u$ and $v$ which are connected by a diagonal. This diagonal will split the graph into two smaller triangulated graphs both containing the edge $uv$. By induction we may color each part with 3 colors where we may choose color 1 for $u$ and color 2 for $v$ in each coloring. Pasting the colorings together yields a 3-coloring of the whole graph.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the triangulation graph is 3-colorable

nodes.name: Base case n = 3
nodes.statement: \textit{This graph is 3-colorable.} For $n = 3$ there is nothing to prove.
nodes.statement_short: Base case n = 3

nodes.name: Split along a diagonal and paste colorings by induction
nodes.statement: Now for $n > 3$ pick any two vertices $u$ and $v$ which are connected by a diagonal. This diagonal will split the graph into two smaller triangulated graphs both containing the edge $uv$. By induction we may color each part with 3 colors where we may choose color 1 for $u$ and color 2 for $v$ in each coloring. Pasting the colorings together yields a 3-coloring of the whole graph.
nodes.statement_short: Split along a diagonal and paste colorings by induction

nodes.name: Guard the smallest color class
nodes.statement: The rest is easy. Since there are $n$ vertices, at least one of the color classes, say the vertices colored 1, contains at most $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{3} \right\rfloor$ vertices, and this is where we place the guards. Since every triangle contains a vertex of color 1 we infer that every triangle is guarded, and hence so is the whole museum.
nodes.statement_short: Guard the smallest color class

nodes.name: Base case n < p
nodes.statement: We use induction on $n$. One easily computes that (1) is true for $n < p$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case n < p

nodes.name: Take a (p-1)-clique A and B = V \ A
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a graph on $V = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}$ without $p$-cliques with a maximal number of edges, where $n \geq p$. $G$ certainly contains $(p - 1)$-cliques, since otherwise we could add edges. Let $A$ be a $(p - 1)$-clique, and set $B := V \setminus A$.
nodes.statement_short: Take a (p-1)-clique A and B = V \ A

nodes.name: Bound e_B and e_{A,B}
nodes.statement: $A$ contains $\binom{p - 1}{2}$ edges, and we now estimate the edge-number $e_B$ in $B$ and the edge-number $e_{A, B}$ between $A$ and $B$. By induction, we have $e_B \leq \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p - 1}\right) (n - p + 1)^2$. Since $G$ has no $p$-clique, every $v_j \in B$ is adjacent to at most $p - 2$ vertices in $A$, and we obtain $e_{A, B} \leq (p - 2)(n - p + 1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound e_B and e_{A,B}

nodes.name: Sum equals the Turán bound
nodes.statement: Altogether, this yields \[ |E| \leq \binom{p - 1}{2} + \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p - 1}\right) (n - p + 1)^2 + (p - 2)(n - p + 1), \] which is precisely $\left(1 - \frac{1}{p - 1}\right) \frac{n^2}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum equals the Turán bound

nodes.name: Neighborhood S of a max-degree vertex
nodes.statement: This proof makes use of the structure of the Turán graphs. Let $v_m \in V$ be a vertex of maximal degree $d_m = \max_{1 \leq j \leq n} d_j$. Denote by $S$ the set of neighbors of $v_m$, $|S| = d_m$, and set $T := V \setminus S$. As $G$ contains no $p$-clique, and $v_m$ is adjacent to all vertices of $S$, we note that $S$ contains no $(p - 1)$-clique.
nodes.statement_short: Neighborhood S of a max-degree vertex

nodes.name: Graph H complete between S and T
nodes.statement: We now construct the following graph $H$ on $V$ (see the figure). $H$ corresponds to $G$ on $S$ and contains all edges between $S$ and $T$, but no edges within $T$. In other words, $T$ is an independent set in $H$, and we conclude that $H$ has again no $p$-cliques.
nodes.statement_short: Graph H complete between S and T

nodes.name: |E(H)| >= |E|
nodes.statement: Let $d'_j$ be the degree of $v_j$ in $H$. If $v_j \in S$, then we certainly have $d'_j \geq d_j$ by the construction of $H$, and for $v_j \in T$, we see $d'_j = |S| = d_m \geq d_j$ by the choice of $v_m$. We infer $|E(H)| \geq |E|$, and find that among all graphs with a maximal number of edges, there must be one of the form of $H$.

nodes.name: Induction gives the bound
nodes.statement: By induction, the graph induced by $S$ has at most as many edges as a suitable graph $K_{n_1, \dots, n_{p - 2}}$ on $S$. So $|E| \leq |E(H)| \leq E(K_{n_1, \dots, n_{p - 1}})$ with $n_{p - 1} = |T|$, which implies (1).
nodes.statement_short: Induction gives the bound

nodes.name: Maximize f(w) over distributions
nodes.statement: Consider a \emph{probability distribution} $\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \dots, w_n)$ on the vertices, that is, an assignment of values $w_i \geq 0$ to the vertices with $\sum_{i=1}^n w_i = 1$. Our goal is to maximize the function \[ f(\mathbf{w}) = \sum_{v_i v_j \in E} w_i w_j. \]
nodes.statement_short: Maximize f(w) over distributions

nodes.name: Moving weight between nonadjacent vertices does not decrease f
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathbf{w}$ is any distribution, and let $v_i$ and $v_j$ be a pair of nonadjacent vertices with positive weights $w_i, w_j$. Let $s_i$ be the sum of the weights of all vertices adjacent to $v_i$, and define $s_j$ similarly for $v_j$, where we may assume that $s_i \geq s_j$. Now we move the weight from $v_j$ to $v_i$, that is, the new weight of $v_i$ is $w_i + w_j$, while the weight of $v_j$ drops to 0. For the new distribution $\mathbf{w'}$ we find \[ f(\mathbf{w'}) = f(\mathbf{w}) + w_j s_i - w_j s_j \geq f(\mathbf{w}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Moving weight between nonadjacent vertices does not decrease f

nodes.name: Optimal weights concentrate on a clique
nodes.statement: We repeat this (reducing the number of vertices with a positive weight by one in each step) until there are no nonadjacent vertices of positive weight anymore. Thus we conclude that there is an optimal distribution whose nonzero weights are concentrated on a clique, say on a $k$-clique.
nodes.statement_short: Optimal weights concentrate on a clique

nodes.name: Uniform weights on the clique are optimal
nodes.statement: Now if, say, $w_1 \geq w_2 > 0$, then choose $w_1' = w_1 - \varepsilon w_1 - w_2$ and change $w_1$ to $w_1 - \varepsilon$ and $w_2$ to $w_2 + \varepsilon$. The new distribution $\mathbf{w'}$ satisfies $f(\mathbf{w'}) = f(\mathbf{w}) + \varepsilon (w_2 s_1 - w_1 s_2) \geq f(\mathbf{w})$, and we infer that the maximal value of $f(\mathbf{w})$ is attained for $w_i = 1/k$ on a $k$-clique and $w_i = 0$ otherwise. Since a $k$-clique contains $\binom{k}{2}$ edges, we obtain \[ f(\mathbf{w}) = \binom{k}{2} \frac{1}{k^2} = \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{k}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Uniform weights on the clique are optimal

nodes.name: f <= (1 - 1/(p-1))/2
nodes.statement: Since this expression is increasing in $k$, the best we can do is to set $k = p - 1$ (since $G$ has no $p$-cliques). So we conclude \[ f(\mathbf{w}) \leq \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p - 1}\right) \] for any distribution $\mathbf{w}$.

nodes.name: Uniform distribution gives Turán's bound
nodes.statement: In particular, this inequality holds for the \emph{uniform} distribution given by $w_i = \frac{1}{n}$ for all $i$. Thus we find \[ \frac{|E|}{n^2} = f\left(\mathbf{w} = \frac{1}{n}\right) \leq \frac{1}{2} \left(1 - \frac{1}{p - 1}\right), \] which is precisely (1).
nodes.statement_short: Uniform distribution gives Turán's bound

nodes.name: Degrees d_i and clique number ω(G)
nodes.statement: This time we use some concepts from probability theory. Let $G$ be an arbitrary graph on the vertex set $V = \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}$. Denote the degree of $v_i$ by $d_i$, and write $\omega(G)$ for the number of vertices in a largest clique, called the clique number of $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Degrees d_i and clique number ω(G)

nodes.name: Cauchy–Schwarz gives n^2 <= ω(G) sum (n - d_i)
nodes.statement: To deduce Turán’s theorem from the claim we use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality from Chapter \ref{chapter20}, \[ \left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i b_i \right)^2 \leq \left( \sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2 \right) \left( \sum_{i=1}^n b_i^2 \right). \] Set $a_i = \sqrt{n - d_i}$, $b_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n - d_i}}$, then $a_i b_i = 1$, and so \[ n^2 \leq \left( \sum_{i=1}^n (n - d_i) \right) \left( \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n - d_i} \right) \leq \omega(G) \sum_{i=1}^n (n - d_i). \tag{2} \]
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy–Schwarz gives n^2 <= ω(G) sum (n - d_i)

nodes.name: ω(G) <= p - 1 and handshaking give Turán
nodes.statement: At this point we apply the hypothesis $\omega(G) \leq p - 1$ of Turán’s theorem. Using also $\sum_{i=1}^n d_i = 2|E|$ from the chapter on double counting, inequality (2) leads to \[ n^2 \leq (p - 1)(n^2 - 2|E|), \] and this is equivalent to Turán’s inequality.
nodes.statement_short: ω(G) <= p - 1 and handshaking give Turán

nodes.name: Random permutation and greedy clique C_π
nodes.statement: We choose a random permutation $\pi = v_1 v_2 \dots v_n$ of the vertex set $V$, where each permutation is supposed to appear with the same probability $\frac{1}{n!}$, and then consider the following set $C_{\pi}$. We put $v_i$ into $C_{\pi}$ if and only if $v_i$ is adjacent to all $v_j$ $(j < i)$ preceding $v_i$. By definition, $C_{\pi}$ is a clique in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Random permutation and greedy clique C_π

nodes.name: P(v_i in C_π) = 1/(n - d_i)
nodes.statement: Let $X = |C_{\pi}|$ be the corresponding random variable. We have $X = \sum_{i=1}^n X_i$, where $X_i$ is the indicator random variable of the vertex $v_i$, that is, $X_i = 1$ or $X_i = 0$ depending on whether $v_i \in C_{\pi}$ or $v_i \notin C_{\pi}$. Note that $v_i$ belongs to $C_{\pi}$ with respect to the permutation $v_1 v_2 \dots v_n$ if and only if $v_i$ appears before all $n - 1 - d_i$ vertices which are not adjacent to $v_i$, or in other words, if $v_i$ is the first among $v_i$ and its $n - 1 - d_i$ non-neighbors. The probability that this happens is $\frac{1}{n - d_i}$, hence $E X_i = \frac{1}{n - d_i}$.
nodes.statement_short: P(v_i in C_π) = 1/(n - d_i)

nodes.name: Expected clique size gives the bound
nodes.statement: Thus by linearity of expectation (see ?) we obtain \[ E(|C_{\pi}|) = E X = \sum_{i=1}^n E X_i = \sum_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{n - d_i}. \] Consequently, there must be a clique of at least that size, and this was our claim.
nodes.statement_short: Expected clique size gives the bound

nodes.name: Take an edge-maximal p-clique-free graph
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a graph on $n$ vertices without a $p$-clique and with a maximal number of edges.
nodes.statement_short: Take an edge-maximal p-clique-free graph

nodes.name: Claim: no vertex is nonadjacent to both ends of an edge
nodes.statement: \textbf{Claim.} \textit{G does not contain three vertices $u$, $v$, $w$ such that $vw \in E$, but $uv \notin E$, $uw \notin E$.} Suppose otherwise, and consider the following cases. \textbf{Case 1:} $d(u) < d(v)$ or $d(u) < d(w)$. We may suppose that $d(u) < d(v)$. Then we duplicate $v$, that is, we create a new vertex $v'$ which has exactly the same neighbors as $v$ (but $v'$ is not an edge), delete $u$, and keep the rest unchanged. The new graph $G'$ has again no $p$-clique, and for the number of edges we find \[ |E(G')| = |E(G)| + d(v) - d(u) > |E(G)|, \] a contradiction. \textbf{Case 2:} $d(u) \geq d(v)$ and $d(u) \geq d(w)$. Duplicate $u$ twice and delete $v$ and $w$ (as illustrated in the margin). Again, the new graph $G'$ has no $p$-clique, and we compute (the $-1$ results from the edge $vw$): \[ |E(G')| = |E(G)| + 2d(u) - (d(v) + d(w) - 1) > |E(G)|. \] So we have a contradiction once more.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: no vertex is nonadjacent to both ends of an edge

nodes.name: Assume such u, v, w exist
nodes.statement: Suppose otherwise, and consider the following cases.
nodes.statement_short: Assume such u, v, w exist

nodes.name: d(u) < d(v): duplicate v, delete u
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1:} $d(u) < d(v)$ or $d(u) < d(w)$. We may suppose that $d(u) < d(v)$. Then we duplicate $v$, that is, we create a new vertex $v'$ which has exactly the same neighbors as $v$ (but $v'$ is not an edge), delete $u$, and keep the rest unchanged. The new graph $G'$ has again no $p$-clique, and for the number of edges we find \[ |E(G')| = |E(G)| + d(v) - d(u) > |E(G)|, \] a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: d(u) < d(v): duplicate v, delete u

nodes.name: d(u) maximal: duplicate u twice, delete v and w
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2:} $d(u) \geq d(v)$ and $d(u) \geq d(w)$. Duplicate $u$ twice and delete $v$ and $w$ (as illustrated in the margin). Again, the new graph $G'$ has no $p$-clique, and we compute (the $-1$ results from the edge $vw$): \[ |E(G')| = |E(G)| + 2d(u) - (d(v) + d(w) - 1) > |E(G)|. \] So we have a contradiction once more.
nodes.statement_short: d(u) maximal: duplicate u twice, delete v and w

nodes.name: Non-adjacency is an equivalence relation: G is complete multipartite
nodes.statement: A moment’s thought shows that the claim we have proved is equivalent to the statement that \[ u \sim v : \iff uv \notin E(G) \] defines an equivalence relation. Thus $G$ is a complete multipartite graph, $G = K_{n_1, \dots, n_{p-1}}$, and we are finished.
nodes.statement_short: Non-adjacency is an equivalence relation: G is complete multipartite

nodes.name: Assume no set contains antipodes; distance map f
nodes.statement: Let a covering $S^d = U_1 \cup \dots \cup U_d \cup U_{d+1}$ be given as specified, and assume that there are no antipodal points in any of the sets $U_i$. We define a map $f : S^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ by \[ f(x) := \big(\delta(x, U_1), \delta(x, U_2), \dots, \delta(x, U_d)\big). \]
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Assume no set contains antipodes; distance map f

nodes.name: f is continuous
nodes.statement: Here $\delta(x, U_i)$ denotes the distance of $x$ from $U_i$. Since this is a continuous function in $x$, the map $f$ is continuous.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: f is continuous

nodes.name: Borsuk–Ulam gives antipodes with δ = 0 for some U_k
nodes.statement: Thus the Borsuk–Ulam theorem tells us that there are antipodal points $x^*, -x^*$ with $f(x^*) = f(-x^*)$. Since $U_{d+1}$ does not contain antipodes, we get that at least one of $x^*$ and $-x^*$ must be contained in one of the sets $U_i$, say in $U_k$ ($k \leq d$). After exchanging $x^*$ with $-x^*$ if necessary, we may assume that $x^* \in U_k$. In particular this yields $\delta(x^*, U_k) = 0$, and from $f(x^*) = f(-x^*)$ we get that $\delta(-x^*, U_k) = 0$ as well.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Borsuk–Ulam gives antipodes with δ = 0 for some U_k

nodes.name: Closed case
nodes.statement: If $U_k$ is closed, then $\delta(-x^*, U_k) = 0$ implies that $-x^* \in U_k$, and we arrive at the contradiction that $U_k$ contains a pair of antipodal points.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Closed case

nodes.name: Open case
nodes.statement: If $U_k$ is open, then $\delta(-x^*, U_k) = 0$ implies that $-x^*$ lies in $\overline{U_k}$, the closure of $U_k$. The set $U_k$, in turn, is contained in $S^d \setminus (\overline{U_k})$, since this is a closed subset of $S^d$ that contains $U_k$. But this means that $-x^*$ lies in $S^d \setminus (\overline{U_k})$, so it cannot lie in $-U_k$, and $x^*$ cannot lie in $U_k$, a contradiction.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Open case

nodes.name: Points in general position; a (d+1)-coloring
nodes.statement: For our ground set let us take $2k + d$ points in general position on the sphere $S^{d+1}$. Suppose the set $V(n, k)$ of all $k$-subsets of this set is partitioned into $d + 1$ classes, $V(n, k) = V_1 \,\dot{\cup} \, \dots \, \dot{\cup} \, V_{d+1}$. We have to find a pair of disjoint $k$-sets $A$ and $B$ that belong to the same class $V_i$.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Points in general position; a (d+1)-coloring

nodes.name: Open sets O_i and closed set C
nodes.statement: For $i = 1, \dots, d + 1$ we set \[ O_i = \{x \in S^{d+1} : \text{the open hemisphere } H_x \text{ with pole } x \text{ contains a } k\text{-set from } V_i\}. \] Clearly, each $O_i$ is an open set. Together, the open sets $O_i$ and the closed set $C = S^{d+1} \setminus (O_1 \cup \dots \cup O_{d+1})$ cover $S^{d+1}$.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Open sets O_i and closed set C

nodes.name: Antipodal points lie in some O_i
nodes.statement: Invoking Lyusternik–Shnirel'man (\ref{lyusternik_shnirelman}) we know that one of these sets contains antipodal points $x^*$ and $-x^*$. This set cannot be $C$! Indeed, if $x^*, -x^* \in C$, then by the definition of the $O_i$'s, the hemispheres $H_{x^*}$ and $H_{-x^*}$ would contain fewer than $k$ points. This means that at least $d + 2$ points would be on the equator $H_{x^*} \cap H_{-x^*}$ with respect to the north pole $x^*$, that is, on a hyperplane through the origin. But this cannot be since the points are in general position. Hence some $O_i$ contains a pair $x^*, -x^*$, so there exist $k$-sets $A$ and $B$ both in class $V_i$, with $A \subset H_{x^*}$ and $B \subset H_{-x^*}$.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: Antipodal points lie in some O_i

nodes.name: The two k-sets are disjoint
nodes.statement: But since we are talking about open hemispheres, $H_{x^*}$ and $H_{-x^*}$ are disjoint, hence $A$ and $B$ are disjoint, and this is the whole proof.
nodes.section: 43 The chromatic number of Kneser graphs
nodes.statement_short: The two k-sets are disjoint

nodes.name: Assume a counterexample; plan in two parts
nodes.statement: Suppose the assertion is false, and $G$ is a counterexample, that is, no vertex of $G$ is adjacent to all other vertices. To derive a contradiction, we proceed in two steps. The first part is combinatorics, and the second part is linear algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Assume a counterexample; plan in two parts

nodes.name: n = k^2 - k + 1
nodes.statement: Summing over the degrees of the $k$ neighbors of $u$ we get $k^2$. Since every vertex (except $u$) has exactly one common neighbor with $u$, we have counted every vertex once, except for $u$, which was counted $k$ times. So the total number of vertices of $G$ is \[ n = k^2 - k + 1. \]

nodes.name: (2) Linear algebra part
nodes.statement: (2) The rest of the proof is a beautiful application of some standard results of linear algebra. Note first that $k$ must be greater than 2, since for $k \leq 2$ only $G = K_1$ and $G = K_3$ are possible by (1), both of which are trivial windmill graphs. Consider the adjacency matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, as defined on page 282. By part (1), any row has exactly $k$ 1's, and by the condition of the theorem, for any two rows there is exactly one column where they both have a 1. Note further that the main diagonal consists of 0's. Hence we have \[ A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} k & 1 & \dots & 1 \\ 1 & k & 1 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & \dots & 1 & k \end{pmatrix} = (k - 1) I + J, \] where $I$ is the identity matrix, and $J$ the matrix of all 1's. It is immediately checked that $J$ has the eigenvalues $n$ (of multiplicity 1) and $0$ (of multiplicity $n - 1$). It follows that $A^2$ has the eigenvalues $k - 1 + n = k^2$ (of multiplicity 1) and $k - 1$ (of multiplicity $n - 1$). Since $A$ is symmetric and hence diagonalizable, we conclude that $A$ has the eigenvalues $k$ (of multiplicity 1) and $\pm \sqrt{k - 1}$. Suppose $r$ of the eigenvalues are equal to $\sqrt{k - 1}$ and $s$ of them are equal to $-\sqrt{k - 1}$, with $r + s = n - 1$. Now we are almost home. Since the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ equals the trace (which is 0), we find \[ k + r\sqrt{k - 1} - s\sqrt{k - 1} = 0, \] and, in particular, $r \neq s$, and \[ \sqrt{k - 1} = \frac{k}{s - r}. \] Now if the square root $\sqrt{m}$ of a natural number $m$ is rational, then it is an integer! An elegant proof for this was presented by Dedekind in 1858: Let $n_0$ be the smallest natural number with $n_0 \sqrt{m} \in \mathbb{N}$. If $\sqrt{m} \not\in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $0 < \sqrt{m} - \ell < 1$. Setting $n_1 := n_0(\sqrt{m} - \ell)$, we find $n_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n_1 \sqrt{m} = n_0 (\sqrt{m} - \ell) \sqrt{m} = n_0 m - \ell (n_0 \sqrt{m}) \in \mathbb{N}$. With $n_1 < n_0$ this yields a contradiction to the choice of $n_0$. Returning to our equation, let us set $h = \sqrt{k - 1} \in \mathbb{N}$, then \[ h(s - r) = k = h^2 + 1. \] Since $h$ divides $h^2 + 1$ and $h^2$, we find that $h$ must be equal to $1$, and thus $k = 2$, which we have already excluded. So we have arrived at a contradiction, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: (2) Linear algebra part

nodes.name: k > 2
nodes.statement: (2) The rest of the proof is a beautiful application of some standard results of linear algebra. Note first that $k$ must be greater than 2, since for $k \leq 2$ only $G = K_1$ and $G = K_3$ are possible by (1), both of which are trivial windmill graphs.

nodes.name: A^2 = (k-1)I + J
nodes.statement: Consider the adjacency matrix $A = (a_{ij})$, as defined on page 282. By part (1), any row has exactly $k$ 1's, and by the condition of the theorem, for any two rows there is exactly one column where they both have a 1. Note further that the main diagonal consists of 0's. Hence we have \[ A^2 = \begin{pmatrix} k & 1 & \dots & 1 \\ 1 & k & 1 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 1 & \dots & 1 & k \end{pmatrix} = (k - 1) I + J, \] where $I$ is the identity matrix, and $J$ the matrix of all 1's.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues of J and A^2
nodes.statement: It is immediately checked that $J$ has the eigenvalues $n$ (of multiplicity 1) and $0$ (of multiplicity $n - 1$). It follows that $A^2$ has the eigenvalues $k - 1 + n = k^2$ (of multiplicity 1) and $k - 1$ (of multiplicity $n - 1$).
nodes.statement_short: Eigenvalues of J and A^2

nodes.name: Trace gives sqrt(k-1) = k/(s-r)
nodes.statement: Since $A$ is symmetric and hence diagonalizable, we conclude that $A$ has the eigenvalues $k$ (of multiplicity 1) and $\pm \sqrt{k - 1}$. Suppose $r$ of the eigenvalues are equal to $\sqrt{k - 1}$ and $s$ of them are equal to $-\sqrt{k - 1}$, with $r + s = n - 1$. Now we are almost home. Since the sum of the eigenvalues of $A$ equals the trace (which is 0), we find \[ k + r\sqrt{k - 1} - s\sqrt{k - 1} = 0, \] and, in particular, $r \neq s$, and \[ \sqrt{k - 1} = \frac{k}{s - r}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Trace gives sqrt(k-1) = k/(s-r)

nodes.name: Rational square roots are integers
nodes.statement: Now if the square root $\sqrt{m}$ of a natural number $m$ is rational, then it is an integer! An elegant proof for this was presented by Dedekind in 1858: Let $n_0$ be the smallest natural number with $n_0 \sqrt{m} \in \mathbb{N}$. If $\sqrt{m} \not\in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $0 < \sqrt{m} - \ell < 1$. Setting $n_1 := n_0(\sqrt{m} - \ell)$, we find $n_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n_1 \sqrt{m} = n_0 (\sqrt{m} - \ell) \sqrt{m} = n_0 m - \ell (n_0 \sqrt{m}) \in \mathbb{N}$. With $n_1 < n_0$ this yields a contradiction to the choice of $n_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Rational square roots are integers

nodes.name: h | h^2 + 1 forces k = 2: contradiction
nodes.statement: Returning to our equation, let us set $h = \sqrt{k - 1} \in \mathbb{N}$, then \[ h(s - r) = k = h^2 + 1. \] Since $h$ divides $h^2 + 1$ and $h^2$, we find that $h$ must be equal to $1$, and thus $k = 2$, which we have already excluded. So we have arrived at a contradiction, and the proof is complete.
nodes.statement_short: h | h^2 + 1 forces k = 2: contradiction

nodes.name: The C_4-condition
nodes.statement: Note first that the condition of the theorem implies that there are no cycles of length 4 in $G$. Let us call this the \emph{$C_4$-condition}.
nodes.statement_short: The C_4-condition

nodes.name: Nonadjacent vertices have equal degree
nodes.statement: We first prove that any two \emph{nonadjacent} vertices $u$ and $v$ have equal degree $d(u) = d(v)$. Suppose $d(u) = k$, where $w_1, \dots, w_k$ are the neighbors of $u$. Exactly one of the $w_i$, say $w_2$, is adjacent to $v$, and $w_2$ is adjacent to exactly one of the other $w_i$'s, say $w_1$, so that we have the situation of the figure to the left. The vertex $v$ has with $w_1$ the common neighbor $w_2$, and with $w_i$ $(i \geq 2)$ a common neighbor $z_i$ $(i \geq 2)$. By the $C_4$-condition, all these $z_i$ must be distinct. We conclude $d(v) \geq k = d(u)$, and thus $d(u) = d(v) = k$ by symmetry.
nodes.statement_short: Nonadjacent vertices have equal degree

nodes.name: Hence G is k-regular
nodes.statement: To finish the proof of (1), observe that any vertex different from $w_2$ is not adjacent to either $u$ or $v$, and hence has degree $k$, by what we already proved. But since $w_2$ also has a non-neighbor, it has degree $k$ as well, and thus $G$ is $k$-regular.
nodes.statement_short: Hence G is k-regular

nodes.name: Least n_0 with n_0 sqrt(m) natural
nodes.statement: An elegant proof for this was presented by Dedekind in 1858: Let $n_0$ be the smallest natural number with $n_0 \sqrt{m} \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: Least n_0 with n_0 sqrt(m) natural

nodes.name: n_1 = n_0(sqrt m - ℓ) has the same property
nodes.statement: If $\sqrt{m} \not\in \mathbb{N}$, then there exists $\ell \in \mathbb{N}$ with $0 < \sqrt{m} - \ell < 1$. Setting $n_1 := n_0(\sqrt{m} - \ell)$, we find $n_1 \in \mathbb{N}$ and $n_1 \sqrt{m} = n_0 (\sqrt{m} - \ell) \sqrt{m} = n_0 m - \ell (n_0 \sqrt{m}) \in \mathbb{N}$.
nodes.statement_short: n_1 = n_0(sqrt m - ℓ) has the same property

nodes.name: Contradicts minimality of n_0
nodes.statement: With $n_1 < n_0$ this yields a contradiction to the choice of $n_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradicts minimality of n_0
